title: Laravel Tinker Tutorial: Test Your Code in the Terminal
excerpt: Master Laravel Tinker to streamline your development workflow. This tutorial explores how to interact with your application's database, test Eloquent queries, and debug logic in real-time directly from your terminal.
content:
Tinker is an interactive shell that loads your entire Laravel application. You can run PHP and Eloquent code line by line and see results instantly, with no routes, controllers, or views required. Instead of building a page just to check whether a query works, you type the query, press Enter, and read the answer. Once you get used to it, Tinker becomes one of the fastest ways to learn Laravel and to debug your own code.

Starting Tinker

php artisan tinker

You'll see a prompt like >. Type PHP, press Enter, and Tinker prints the result. Everything your application can do is available here: your models, your config, your helpers, your services, and your database connection.

Tinker is built on a PHP shell called PsySH, so you also get a few handy built-in commands:

Command What It Does help Lists available commands ls Shows the variables you've defined in this session show Displays the code of the last exception's location history Shows the commands you've typed exit Leaves Tinker (Ctrl+C also works)

Multi-line input works too. If you open a bracket or a closure and press Enter, Tinker waits for you to finish the statement before running it.

One important behavior to remember: Tinker loads your code once, when it starts. If you edit a model or a class while Tinker is open, the shell will not notice. Type exit and start it again to pick up your changes.

Basic Examples

> 2 + 2
= 4

> now()
= Illuminate\Support\Carbon @1767225600 {...}

> Str::slug('Hello Laravel World')
= "hello-laravel-world"

The = sign in front of a line is Tinker showing you the return value of what you just typed. Every expression returns something, and Tinker prints it. If you want to keep a result, store it in a variable and reuse it on the next line:

> $slug = Str::slug('My First Post');
> strtoupper($slug)
= "MY-FIRST-POST"

This variable-based style is the heart of how you'll use Tinker: build small pieces, check each one, and combine them.

Querying Your Database

> App\Models\User::count()
> App\Models\User::first()
> App\Models\Product::where('price', '>', 100)->get()

Each of these runs against the database defined in your .env file and prints the models it finds. Tinker formats Eloquent results so you can read the attributes of each record directly in the terminal.

Tip: to avoid typing the full namespace each time, you can write use App\Models\Product; at the Tinker prompt first. After that, Product::count() works for the rest of the session. In many projects Tinker also resolves short class names automatically, so try the short name first and fall back to the full namespace if you see a "class not found" message.

Querying in Tinker is the best way to learn Eloquent. You can try where, orderBy, pluck, first, and find one at a time and watch exactly what each returns, before you place any of them inside a controller.

Creating Records

> use App\Models\Product;
> Product::create(['name' => 'Test Mouse', 'price' => 19.99]);

Remember that create() requires the fields to be in your model's $fillable array. If they aren't, Laravel throws a mass assignment error, and Tinker is a great place to discover that quickly and fix it.

You can also create a record in two steps, which is useful when you want to inspect it before saving:

> $product = new Product;
> $product->name = 'Test Keyboard';
> $product->price = 49.99;
> $product->save();

After save(), the model has its new id and timestamps, so typing $product shows you the saved record.

Generating Fake Data

If you've set up factories:

> Product::factory()->count(20)->create();

This inserts 20 realistic products in one line, which is perfect for testing pagination, search, and sorting. If you only want to see what a factory would produce without saving anything, use make() instead of create():

> Product::factory()->make();

make() builds the model in memory and does not touch the database.

Updating and Deleting

> $product = Product::find(1);
> $product->price = 24.99;
> $product->save();

> $product->delete();

You can also update in one step:

> Product::find(1)->update(['price' => 24.99]);

If your model uses soft deletes, delete() only marks the record as deleted. You can bring it back, which is a nice thing to experiment with safely:

> Product::withTrashed()->find(1)->restore();

Testing Relationships

> $user = User::find(1);
> $user->posts;
> $user->posts()->count();
> $user->posts()->create(['title' => 'Created from Tinker']);

Notice the difference between $user->posts (without parentheses) and $user->posts() (with parentheses). The first loads the related records as a collection. The second gives you the relationship query itself, so you can keep adding conditions like where, count, or create. Seeing both side by side in Tinker makes this much easier to understand than reading about it.

You can also check eager loading:

> User::with('posts')->first();

Testing Helpers, Collections, and Dates

> collect([1, 2, 3])->map(fn ($n) => $n * 2)
> now()->addDays(7)->format('Y-m-d')
> Hash::make('secret')

Tinker is ideal for testing small pieces of logic: a date calculation, a string transformation, or a collection chain. Instead of refreshing a browser to see whether diffForHumans() outputs what you expect, you try it in a second:

> now()->subHours(3)->diffForHumans()
= "3 hours ago"

Testing Services and Classes

> app(App\Services\InvoiceService::class)->calculateTotal(100)

Calling app() with a class name asks Laravel's service container to build the object for you, including any dependencies it needs. This lets you test your own classes in isolation, with real inputs, before wiring them into a controller.

Useful Tinker Habits

Habit Why Try a query in Tinker before putting it in a controller Catch typos and logic errors quickly Check ->toSql() on a query See the SQL Laravel generates Use exit or Ctrl+C to leave Returns you to the terminal Restart Tinker after editing code It doesn't reload changed files Store results in variables Lets you reuse and inspect them step by step

Seeing the SQL:

> Product::where('price', '>', 100)->toSql()
= "select * from `products` where `price` > ?"

toSql() shows placeholders instead of real values. In recent Laravel versions, toRawSql() fills the values in, which is easier to read. When a page is slow or a query returns the wrong rows, comparing the generated SQL with what you expected is often the quickest way to find the problem.

Safety Warning

Tinker runs against whatever database your .env points to. If you're connected to a production database, creating or deleting records is real. Treat Tinker on a live server with care. Before running anything that changes data, check which environment you're in:

> app()->environment()
= "local"

A good habit on any server: read first, change second, and never run a destructive command you haven't tested locally.

title: Laravel Breeze vs Jetstream vs Fortify
excerpt: Choosing the right authentication scaffolding for your Laravel project is critical. This guide compares Laravel Breeze, Jetstream, and Fortify, breaking down their unique features, architectural differences, and use cases to help you decide which package best suits your application's complexity.
content:
Laravel offers several official authentication tools, and the names alone can be confusing. This guide explains what each one does and helps you choose.

The Short Version

Package What It Is Includes UI? Breeze Minimal starter kit: login, register, reset, verify, profile Yes Jetstream Feature-rich starter kit: adds teams, 2FA, API tokens, session management Yes Fortify Backend-only authentication engine No Sanctum API token and SPA authentication No

Note: newer Laravel releases also ship updated official starter kits for React, Vue, and Livewire. The ideas below still apply, but check the current Laravel documentation for the newest installer options.

Laravel Breeze

Breeze is the simplest way to get working authentication. Its code is published directly into your app, so you can read and edit every file.

composer require laravel/breeze --dev
php artisan breeze:install

Best for: beginners, small to medium apps, and anyone who wants to understand how auth works.

Laravel Jetstream

Jetstream builds on Fortify and adds extras:

  • Two-factor authentication

  • Browser session management

  • Team management

  • API token management (via Sanctum)

composer require laravel/jetstream
php artisan jetstream:install livewire

Best for: SaaS-style apps that need teams and 2FA from day one.

Trade-off: more files, more concepts, and more to learn before you can customize it confidently.

Laravel Fortify

Fortify provides the backend logic (routes and controllers for login, registration, password reset, 2FA) but no views. You build your own frontend.

composer require laravel/fortify
php artisan fortify:install

Best for: projects with a fully custom design or a separate frontend that still wants Laravel's battle-tested auth logic.

Laravel Sanctum

Sanctum isn't a login UI. It's the token system for APIs and SPAs. You'll often use it alongside one of the others.

Best for: mobile app backends and JavaScript frontends.

Decision Guide

Your Situation Choose Learning Laravel, building a first project Breeze Need teams, 2FA, and profile photos out of the box Jetstream Custom UI design, no prebuilt views wanted Fortify Mobile app or separate frontend calling your API Sanctum Blade site that also exposes an API Breeze + Sanctum

Can You Switch Later?

Yes, but it takes work. Breeze publishes its code into your project, so moving to something else means rewriting parts of it. Choose thoughtfully at the start, but don't be paralyzed. For most beginners, Breeze is a safe starting point.

title: Laravel Sanctum Tutorial: API Authentication Made Simple
excerpt: Learn how to implement secure, lightweight API authentication in your Laravel applications using Sanctum. This guide covers everything from initial setup and token issuance to protecting routes for SPAs and mobile clients with practical code examples.
content:
When a mobile app or JavaScript frontend talks to your Laravel API, it can't use browser sessions the usual way. Laravel Sanctum provides lightweight token-based authentication that's perfect for beginners.

What Sanctum Offers

  • API tokens for mobile apps and third-party clients

  • Cookie-based session auth for single-page apps on the same domain

This tutorial focuses on API tokens.

Step 1: Install Sanctum

php artisan install:api

This installs Sanctum, creates routes/api.php, and adds the token migration. Then run:

php artisan migrate

Step 2: Add the Trait to Your User Model

use Laravel\Sanctum\HasApiTokens;

class User extends Authenticatable
{
    use HasApiTokens, Notifiable;
}

Step 3: Build the Register Endpoint

use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Hash;

public function register(Request $request)
{
    $data = $request->validate([
        'name' => 'required|string|max:255',
        'email' => 'required|email|unique:users',
        'password' => 'required|min:8|confirmed',
    ]);

    $user = User::create([
        'name' => $data['name'],
        'email' => $data['email'],
        'password' => Hash::make($data['password']),
    ]);

    $token = $user->createToken('mobile-app')->plainTextToken;

    return response()->json(['user' => $user, 'token' => $token], 201);
}

Step 4: Build the Login Endpoint

public function login(Request $request)
{
    $data = $request->validate([
        'email' => 'required|email',
        'password' => 'required',
    ]);

    $user = User::where('email', $data['email'])->first();

    if (! $user || ! Hash::check($data['password'], $user->password)) {
        return response()->json(['message' => 'Invalid credentials'], 401);
    }

    $token = $user->createToken('mobile-app')->plainTextToken;

    return response()->json(['user' => $user, 'token' => $token]);
}

Step 5: Protect Routes

routes/api.php

use App\Http\Controllers\AuthController;
use App\Http\Controllers\Api\ProductController;

Route::post('/register', [AuthController::class, 'register']);
Route::post('/login', [AuthController::class, 'login']);

Route::middleware('auth:sanctum')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/user', fn (Request $request) => $request->user());
    Route::post('/logout', [AuthController::class, 'logout']);
    Route::apiResource('products', ProductController::class);
});

Step 6: Logout (Revoke the Token)

public function logout(Request $request)
{
    $request->user()->currentAccessToken()->delete();

    return response()->json(['message' => 'Logged out']);
}

To revoke every token for the user:

$request->user()->tokens()->delete();

Calling the API With a Token

The client sends the token in the Authorization header:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/user \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer 1|abcdef123456..." \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

Always send Accept: application/json, otherwise Laravel may redirect failed auth attempts to a login page instead of returning a JSON 401.

Token Abilities (Simple Permissions)

$token = $user->createToken('reports', ['reports:read'])->plainTextToken;

if ($request->user()->tokenCan('reports:read')) {
    // allowed
}

Common Mistakes

Mistake Fix Getting an HTML login page instead of JSON Add the Accept: application/json header 401 on every request Check the header format: Bearer <token> with a space Storing the token in plain view on the client Use secure storage on mobile apps Forgetting HasApiTokens createToken() will not exist without it

title: Laravel Livewire Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Learn how to build dynamic, reactive interfaces in Laravel without leaving the comfort of PHP. This tutorial covers the fundamentals of Livewire, from component lifecycle management to real-time data binding, helping you streamline your full-stack development workflow.
content:
Livewire lets you build interactive interfaces (live counters, search-as-you-type, forms without page reloads) using only PHP and Blade. It's a great fit if you know Laravel but don't want to learn a JavaScript framework yet.

How Livewire Works

You write a PHP class (the component) and a Blade view. When the user interacts with the page, Livewire sends a small request to the server, runs your PHP method, and updates only the changed part of the page.

Step 1: Install Livewire

composer require livewire/livewire

Step 2: Create a Component

php artisan make:livewire counter

This creates a class and a view:

app/Livewire/Counter.php
resources/views/livewire/counter.blade.php

Step 3: Write the Component Class

namespace App\Livewire;

use Livewire\Component;

class Counter extends Component
{
    public int $count = 0;

    public function increment()
    {
        $this->count++;
    }

    public function decrement()
    {
        $this->count--;
    }

    public function render()
    {
        return view('livewire.counter');
    }
}

Public properties are automatically available in the view and stay in sync with the browser.

Step 4: Write the View

<div>
    <button wire:click="decrement">-</button>
    <span>{{ $count }}</span>
    <button wire:click="increment">+</button>
</div>

A Livewire view must have exactly one root element.

Step 5: Use the Component in a Page

<livewire:counter />

The counter now updates instantly with no page reload and no JavaScript written by you.

Live Search Example

class ProductSearch extends Component
{
    public string $search = '';

    public function render()
    {
        return view('livewire.product-search', [
            'products' => Product::where('name', 'like', "%{$this->search}%")
                ->take(10)
                ->get(),
        ]);
    }
}

<div>
    <input type="text" wire:model.live="search" placeholder="Search products...">

    <ul>
        @foreach ($products as $product)
            <li>{{ $product->name }}</li>
        @endforeach
    </ul>
</div>

wire:model.live updates the list as the user types.

Handling Forms With Validation

use Livewire\Attributes\Validate;

class CreateTask extends Component
{
    #[Validate('required|min:3')]
    public string $title = '';

    public function save()
    {
        $this->validate();

        Task::create(['title' => $this->title]);

        $this->reset('title');
        session()->flash('success', 'Task created!');
    }

    public function render()
    {
        return view('livewire.create-task');
    }
}

<form wire:submit="save">
    <input type="text" wire:model="title">
    @error('title') <span>{{ $message }}</span> @enderror

    <button type="submit">Add Task</button>
</form>

Common Livewire Directives

Directive Purpose wire:click Call a method on click wire:model Bind an input to a property (syncs on next request) wire:model.live Bind and sync as the user types wire:submit Handle a form submission wire:loading Show an element while a request is running wire:confirm Ask for confirmation before an action

Livewire vs Plain Blade vs a JavaScript Framework

Choose When Plain Blade Mostly static pages with simple forms Livewire Interactive features, and your team prefers staying in PHP Vue/React Highly interactive apps, or a separate frontend consuming an API

title: Laravel .env File Explained: Environment Configuration for Beginners
excerpt: Master Laravel environment configuration by understanding how the .env file manages sensitive credentials and application settings. This guide breaks down key-value pairs, environment variables, and security best practices for production-ready web applications.
content:
Your local machine and your live server need different settings: different database passwords, different debug modes, different mail servers. Laravel solves this with the .env file and the config/ folder.

What is the .env File?

It's a plain-text file in your project root containing key-value pairs:

APP_NAME=MyShop
APP_ENV=local
APP_KEY=base64:xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
APP_DEBUG=true
APP_URL=http://localhost

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_DATABASE=myshop
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=

Each environment (local, staging, production) has its own .env file with its own values.

.env vs .env.example

  • .env holds real values and is never committed to Git

  • .env.example is a template with empty or dummy values, which is committed so teammates know what variables are needed

When setting up a project:

cp .env.example .env
php artisan key:generate

Important Variables

Variable Purpose APP_ENV local, staging, or production APP_DEBUG Show detailed errors (true locally, false in production) APP_KEY Encryption key used for sessions and cookies APP_URL Base URL of your app DB_* Database connection settings MAIL_* Mail server settings QUEUE_CONNECTION Queue driver

Reading Values: env() vs config()

You can read an environment variable with env():

$debug = env('APP_DEBUG');

But the recommended pattern is to read it only inside config files, and use config() everywhere else.

config/services.php

return [
    'payment' => [
        'key' => env('PAYMENT_API_KEY'),
    ],
];

Anywhere else in your app

$key = config('services.payment.key');

Why Not Use env() Everywhere?

When you run php artisan config:cache in production, Laravel stops loading the .env file. Any env() call outside config files will return null. Using config() always works, cached or not.

Creating Your Own Config File

config/shop.php

return [
    'currency' => env('SHOP_CURRENCY', 'USD'),
    'items_per_page' => 12,
];

echo config('shop.currency'); // USD

The second argument to env() is a default value used when the variable isn't set.

Checking the Current Environment

if (app()->environment('production')) {
    // production-only logic
}

Values With Spaces

Wrap them in quotes:

APP_NAME="My Online Shop"

Common Mistakes

Mistake Fix Changes to .env not taking effect Run php artisan config:clear env() returns null in production Move the env() call into a config file and use config() .env committed to Git Add it to .gitignore and rotate any exposed passwords "No application encryption key" error Run php artisan key:generate

title: Laravel Query Builder vs Eloquent: What's the Difference?
excerpt: Struggling to choose between Laravel Query Builder and Eloquent ORM? Explore the key performance differences, syntax trade-offs, and architectural use cases to determine which database approach is right for your next project.
content:
Laravel gives you two ways to talk to your database: the Query Builder and Eloquent ORM. Beginners often wonder which one to use. This article compares them side by side so you can choose confidently.

What is the Query Builder?

The Query Builder is a fluent interface for building SQL queries using PHP methods. It works directly with tables and returns plain objects (stdClass), not models.

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

$products = DB::table('products')
    ->where('price', '>', 100)
    ->orderBy('name')
    ->get();

What is Eloquent?

Eloquent maps each table to a Model class. Results come back as model instances with built-in features like relationships, accessors, and events.

$products = Product::where('price', '>', 100)
    ->orderBy('name')
    ->get();

Notice that the syntax is almost identical. The difference is what happens behind the scenes.

Side-by-Side Examples

Task Query Builder Eloquent Get all rows DB::table('products')->get() Product::all() Find by ID DB::table('products')->find(1) Product::find(1) Insert DB::table('products')->insert([...]) Product::create([...]) Update DB::table('products')->where('id', 1)->update([...]) $product->update([...]) Delete DB::table('products')->where('id', 1)->delete() $product->delete()

Key Differences

Feature Query Builder Eloquent Returns Plain stdClass objects Model instances Relationships Manual joins hasMany, belongsTo, etc. Timestamps Manual Automatic (created_at, updated_at) Soft deletes Manual Built in via trait Accessors/mutators No Yes Model events No Yes Speed Slightly faster (less overhead) Slightly slower, much more convenient

Joins With the Query Builder

$orders = DB::table('orders')
    ->join('users', 'users.id', '=', 'orders.user_id')
    ->select('orders.id', 'users.name', 'orders.total')
    ->get();

The Eloquent equivalent uses relationships:

$orders = Order::with('user')->get();

Aggregates and Reports

The Query Builder shines for reporting queries that don't map neatly to a single model:

$sales = DB::table('orders')
    ->select(DB::raw('DATE(created_at) as day, SUM(total) as revenue'))
    ->groupBy('day')
    ->get();

Raw Expressions (Use With Care)

$products = DB::table('products')
    ->whereRaw('price > ? AND stock < ?', [100, 5])
    ->get();

Always use bound parameters (the ? placeholders) to prevent SQL injection. Never concatenate user input into raw SQL.

Which Should You Use?

  • Use Eloquent for everyday work: CRUD, relationships, anything tied to a model. This is the default choice for most beginners.

  • Use the Query Builder for complex reports, bulk operations, or tables that have no model.

  • You can mix both in the same project without any problem.

title: Laravel Error Handling and Custom Error Pages Tutorial
excerpt: Master Laravel error handling by learning to implement custom exception reporting, configuration, and branded error pages. This tutorial provides practical examples for creating user-friendly 404 and 500 status pages to improve your application's reliability and professional UX.
content:
Errors are inevitable — a missing page, a failed database query, an unexpected input. What matters is how gracefully your app handles them. This tutorial covers Laravel's exception handling system and building custom error pages.

How Laravel Handles Errors by Default

When an error occurs, Laravel catches it through its exception handler and:

  • In development (APP_DEBUG=true): shows a detailed error page with the stack trace

  • In production (APP_DEBUG=false): shows a clean, generic error page and logs the details instead

Where Errors Are Logged

storage/logs/laravel.log

Every unhandled exception gets written here with a full stack trace — this is the first place to check when something breaks in production.

Manually Throwing Exceptions

if (! $product) {
    abort(404, 'Product not found');
}

throw new \Exception('Something went wrong processing this order.');

Common HTTP Error Codes

Code Meaning When to Use 403 Forbidden User isn't authorized to do this 404 Not Found Resource doesn't exist 419 Page Expired CSRF token mismatch 422 Unprocessable Entity Validation failed 429 Too Many Requests Rate limit exceeded 500 Server Error Unexpected application error

Building Custom Error Pages

Laravel looks for views matching the error code inside resources/views/errors/.

php artisan vendor:publish --tag=laravel-errors

This publishes default error views you can customize:

resources/views/errors/
├── 404.blade.php
├── 403.blade.php
├── 500.blade.php

resources/views/errors/404.blade.php

@extends('layouts.app')

@section('content')
    <div class="text-center py-20">
        <h1 class="text-4xl font-bold">Page Not Found</h1>
        <p class="mt-4">Sorry, we couldn't find the page you're looking for.</p>
        <a href="{{ url('/') }}" class="mt-6 inline-block text-blue-600">Go back home</a>
    </div>
@endsection

Handling Specific Exceptions

In bootstrap/app.php (Laravel 11+), you can customize how specific exception types are handled:

->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions) {
    $exceptions->render(function (ModelNotFoundException $e, Request $request) {
        if ($request->wantsJson()) {
            return response()->json(['message' => 'Resource not found.'], 404);
        }
    });
})

Try/Catch for Expected Failures

try {
    $result = $this->paymentGateway->charge($order->total);
} catch (PaymentFailedException $e) {
    Log::error('Payment failed: ' . $e->getMessage());

    return redirect()->back()->with('error', 'Payment could not be processed. Please try again.');
}

Custom Exception Classes

php artisan make:exception InsufficientStockException

class InsufficientStockException extends \Exception
{
    public function __construct(public Product $product)
    {
        parent::__construct("Not enough stock for {$product->name}");
    }
}

Usage:

if ($product->stock < $requestedQuantity) {
    throw new InsufficientStockException($product);
}

Returning JSON Errors for APIs

public function render($request, Throwable $exception)
{
    if ($request->is('api/*')) {
        return response()->json([
            'message' => $exception->getMessage(),
        ], 500);
    }

    return parent::render($request, $exception);
}

Logging Levels

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log;

Log::info('User logged in.');
Log::warning('Low stock detected.');
Log::error('Payment gateway timeout.');
Log::critical('Database connection lost.');

Using appropriate log levels makes it much easier to filter and monitor logs later, especially with external tools like Sentry or Papertrail.

Debugging Checklist

  • [ ] Check storage/logs/laravel.log first

  • [ ] Confirm APP_DEBUG is set correctly for the environment

  • [ ] Use dd() or dump() to inspect variables during development

  • [ ] Wrap risky operations (payments, external APIs) in try/catch blocks

  • [ ] Never expose raw exception messages to end users in production

title: Laravel Relationships Tutorial: One-to-Many and Many-to-Many Explained
excerpt: Master Laravel Eloquent relationships with this comprehensive guide. Learn how to implement one-to-many, many-to-many, polymorphic, and through relationships with practical code examples and database schema best practices.
content:
Real applications are built on connected data — a user has many orders, a product belongs to many categories, a post has one author. This tutorial dives deeper into Eloquent's relationship types with practical, real-world examples.

One-to-One

Example: a User has one Profile.

// User.php
public function profile()
{
    return $this->hasOne(Profile::class);
}

// Profile.php
public function user()
{
    return $this->belongsTo(User::class);
}

Migration for profiles:

Schema::create('profiles', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->foreignId('user_id')->constrained();
    $table->string('bio')->nullable();
    $table->timestamps();
});

Usage:

$bio = $user->profile->bio;

One-to-Many

Example: a User has many Posts.

// User.php
public function posts()
{
    return $this->hasMany(Post::class);
}

// Post.php
public function user()
{
    return $this->belongsTo(User::class);
}

Migration for posts:

Schema::create('posts', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->foreignId('user_id')->constrained()->onDelete('cascade');
    $table->string('title');
    $table->timestamps();
});

Usage:

$posts = $user->posts;

// Creating a related post directly
$user->posts()->create(['title' => 'My First Post']);

Many-to-Many

Example: a Product belongs to many Categories, and a Category has many Products.

This requires a pivot table — a table that only exists to link the two.

php artisan make:migration create_category_product_table

Schema::create('category_product', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->foreignId('category_id')->constrained()->onDelete('cascade');
    $table->foreignId('product_id')->constrained()->onDelete('cascade');
    $table->timestamps();
});

Laravel expects pivot tables to be named alphabetically using the two model names, singular, joined with an underscore: category_product.

// Product.php
public function categories()
{
    return $this->belongsToMany(Category::class);
}

// Category.php
public function products()
{
    return $this->belongsToMany(Product::class);
}

Attaching and Detaching Relationships

$product->categories()->attach($categoryId);
$product->categories()->detach($categoryId);

// Replace all existing categories with a new set
$product->categories()->sync([1, 2, 3]);

Accessing Pivot Data

If your pivot table has extra columns (like quantity on an order_items table):

public function products()
{
    return $this->belongsToMany(Product::class)->withPivot('quantity');
}

foreach ($order->products as $product) {
    echo $product->pivot->quantity;
}

Has-Many-Through

Example: a Country has many Posts through Users.

public function posts()
{
    return $this->hasManyThrough(Post::class, User::class);
}

$posts = $country->posts; // all posts written by users in this country

Polymorphic Relationships

Example: both Post and Video can have Comments, using a single comments table.

Schema::create('comments', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->text('body');
    $table->morphs('commentable'); // adds commentable_id and commentable_type
    $table->timestamps();
});

// Comment.php
public function commentable()
{
    return $this->morphTo();
}

// Post.php
public function comments()
{
    return $this->morphMany(Comment::class, 'commentable');
}

// Video.php
public function comments()
{
    return $this->morphMany(Comment::class, 'commentable');
}

$post->comments()->create(['body' => 'Great article!']);
$video->comments()->create(['body' => 'Awesome video!']);

Relationship Types Summary

Relationship Example Method One-to-One User → Profile hasOne / belongsTo One-to-Many User → Posts hasMany / belongsTo Many-to-Many Product ↔ Category belongsToMany Has-Many-Through Country → Posts (via Users) hasManyThrough Polymorphic Post/Video → Comments morphMany / morphTo

title: Laravel Seeders and Factories Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Learn how to streamline your Laravel development workflow by using Seeders and Factories to populate your database with realistic, automated test data. This guide covers defining model factories, utilizing the Faker library, handling complex relationships, and organizing bulk data insertion with custom seeders.
content:
Testing your app with an empty database is painful — you can't see how a product list looks with 50 items, or test pagination with only 2 rows. Laravel's Seeders and Factories let you generate realistic fake data instantly.

Factories: Defining What Fake Data Looks Like

A factory describes how to generate a fake version of a model.

Creating a Factory

php artisan make:factory ProductFactory --model=Product

Defining the Factory

database/factories/ProductFactory.php

namespace Database\Factories;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Factories\Factory;

class ProductFactory extends Factory
{
    public function definition(): array
    {
        return [
            'name' => fake()->words(3, true),
            'description' => fake()->sentence(),
            'price' => fake()->randomFloat(2, 10, 500),
            'is_active' => fake()->boolean(80), // 80% chance of true
        ];
    }
}

Laravel uses the Faker library under the hood to generate realistic names, sentences, numbers, dates, emails, and more.

Useful Faker Methods

Method Generates fake()->name() A random full name fake()->email() A random email address fake()->sentence() A random sentence fake()->paragraph() A random paragraph fake()->randomFloat(2, 10, 500) A decimal number between 10–500 fake()->boolean() true/false fake()->date() A random date fake()->imageUrl() A placeholder image URL

Using a Factory Directly (in Tinker or a Test)

php artisan tinker

>>> App\Models\Product::factory()->create();
>>> App\Models\Product::factory()->count(50)->create();

This inserts 50 fake products straight into your database.

Factory States (Variations)

public function outOfStock(): Factory
{
    return $this->state(fn (array $attributes) => [
        'is_active' => false,
    ]);
}

Product::factory()->outOfStock()->count(5)->create();

Factories With Relationships

If a Product belongs to a Category:

public function definition(): array
{
    return [
        'name' => fake()->words(3, true),
        'price' => fake()->randomFloat(2, 10, 500),
        'category_id' => \App\Models\Category::factory(),
    ];
}

This automatically creates a related category for every product, unless one is explicitly provided.

Seeders: Running Factories (and Fixed Data) in Bulk

Seeders are scripts that populate your database — often used with factories, but also great for fixed reference data (like default roles or categories).

Creating a Seeder

php artisan make:seeder ProductSeeder

Defining the Seeder

namespace Database\Seeders;

use App\Models\Product;
use Illuminate\Database\Seeder;

class ProductSeeder extends Seeder
{
    public function run(): void
    {
        Product::factory()->count(50)->create();
    }
}

Registering Seeders in the Main Seeder

database/seeders/DatabaseSeeder.php

public function run(): void
{
    $this->call([
        ProductSeeder::class,
        CategorySeeder::class,
    ]);
}

Running Seeders

php artisan db:seed

Run a specific seeder only:

php artisan db:seed --class=ProductSeeder

Reset and re-seed everything at once (development only):

php artisan migrate:fresh --seed

Seeding Fixed Reference Data

class CategorySeeder extends Seeder
{
    public function run(): void
    {
        $categories = ['Electronics', 'Clothing', 'Books', 'Home & Garden'];

        foreach ($categories as $category) {
            Category::create(['name' => $category]);
        }
    }
}

title: Laravel Vite Tutorial: Managing CSS and JavaScript Assets
excerpt: Learn how to streamline your frontend workflow in Laravel by mastering Vite. This guide covers asset compilation, hot module replacement (HMR), and best practices for managing CSS and JavaScript in modern Laravel applications.
content:
Modern Laravel apps use Vite to compile and bundle CSS and JavaScript. This tutorial explains what Vite does, how it's configured, and how to work with it day to day.

What Does Vite Do?

Vite takes your raw CSS/JS source files (in resources/css and resources/js) and compiles them into optimized files the browser can efficiently load — combining files, minifying code, and enabling instant hot-reloading during development.

Project Structure

resources/
├── css/
│   └── app.css
└── js/
    └── app.js

The Vite Config File

vite.config.js

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import laravel from 'laravel-vite-plugin';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [
        laravel({
            input: ['resources/css/app.css', 'resources/js/app.js'],
            refresh: true,
        }),
    ],
});

refresh: true automatically reloads the browser when you edit a Blade file.

Loading Assets in Blade

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    @vite(['resources/css/app.css', 'resources/js/app.js'])
</head>
<body>
    <!-- content -->
</body>
</html>

The @vite directive automatically points to the right compiled files, whether you're in development or production.

Running Vite in Development

npm run dev

This starts a local dev server with hot module replacement — edit your CSS or JS, and the browser updates instantly without a full page reload.

Keep this running in a separate terminal tab alongside php artisan serve.

Building for Production

npm run build

This compiles and minifies everything into public/build/ — this is the step you run before deploying.

Adding Tailwind CSS

npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite

vite.config.js

import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [
        laravel({ input: ['resources/css/app.css', 'resources/js/app.js'], refresh: true }),
        tailwindcss(),
    ],
});

resources/css/app.css

@import "tailwindcss";

Now you can use Tailwind utility classes directly in your Blade files:

<button class="bg-blue-600 text-white px-4 py-2 rounded">
    Save
</button>

Importing JavaScript Libraries

npm install alpinejs

resources/js/app.js

import Alpine from 'alpinejs';

window.Alpine = Alpine;
Alpine.start();

Using Vite With React or Vue

npm install vue @vitejs/plugin-vue

import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [
        laravel({ input: ['resources/css/app.css', 'resources/js/app.js'], refresh: true }),
        vue(),
    ],
});

Common Errors and Fixes

Error Fix "Vite manifest not found" Run npm run build (production) or make sure npm run dev is running (local) Styles not updating Restart npm run dev, or clear the browser cache @vite directive shows nothing Ensure resources/css/app.css and resources/js/app.js paths match your vite.config.js

title: Laravel Authorization Tutorial: Gates and Policies Explained
excerpt: Master Laravel authorization with our comprehensive guide to Gates and Policies. Learn how to secure your application by implementing robust, scalable access control logic for user roles and permissions.
content:
Authentication answers "who is this user?" — authorization answers "what is this user allowed to do?" Laravel gives you two tools for this: Gates (simple, closure-based checks) and Policies (organized, model-specific rules).

Gates: Simple Authorization Checks

Gates are best for actions not tied to a specific model — like "can this user access the admin panel?"

Defining a Gate

In app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Gate;

public function boot(): void
{
    Gate::define('access-admin-panel', function ($user) {
        return $user->is_admin;
    });
}

Checking a Gate

if (Gate::allows('access-admin-panel')) {
    // allowed
}

if (Gate::denies('access-admin-panel')) {
    // not allowed
}

In a Controller

public function index()
{
    if (! Gate::allows('access-admin-panel')) {
        abort(403);
    }

    return view('admin.dashboard');
}

In a Blade View

@can('access-admin-panel')
    <a href="/admin">Admin Panel</a>
@endcan

Policies: Organized, Model-Specific Authorization

Policies are the better choice when your rules revolve around a specific model — like "can this user edit THIS post?"

Step 1: Create a Policy

php artisan make:policy PostPolicy --model=Post

Step 2: Define the Rules

namespace App\Policies;

use App\Models\Post;
use App\Models\User;

class PostPolicy
{
    public function update(User $user, Post $post): bool
    {
        return $user->id === $post->user_id;
    }

    public function delete(User $user, Post $post): bool
    {
        return $user->id === $post->user_id || $user->is_admin;
    }
}

Laravel automatically discovers policies for models following the naming convention (Post → PostPolicy), so no manual registration is usually needed in recent Laravel versions.

Step 3: Checking a Policy in a Controller

public function update(Request $request, Post $post)
{
    $this->authorize('update', $post);

    $post->update($request->validated());

    return redirect()->route('posts.index');
}

If the policy returns false, authorize() automatically throws a 403 error — no manual if check needed.

Checking a Policy in Blade

@can('update', $post)
    <a href="{{ route('posts.edit', $post) }}">Edit</a>
@endcan

@can('delete', $post)
    <form action="{{ route('posts.destroy', $post) }}" method="POST">
        @csrf
        @method('DELETE')
        <button type="submit">Delete</button>
    </form>
@endcan

Checking a Policy Directly on the User

if ($request->user()->can('update', $post)) {
    // ...
}

Policy Methods for Every CRUD Action

By convention, policies typically define these methods:

Method Corresponds To viewAny Viewing a list of records view Viewing a single record create Creating a new record update Editing a record delete Deleting a record restore Restoring a soft-deleted record forceDelete Permanently deleting a record

Giving Admins Automatic Access to Everything

Instead of adding || $user->is_admin to every single policy method, use before():

public function before(User $user, string $ability): bool|null
{
    if ($user->is_admin) {
        return true;
    }

    return null; // fall through to the specific policy method
}

Gates vs Policies: When to Use Which

Use a Gate When... Use a Policy When... The check isn't tied to a specific model You're authorizing actions on a specific model (Post, Order, Product) It's a simple, app-wide permission You have several related rules (view, update, delete) for one model

title: Laravel Localization Tutorial: Building a Multi-Language App
excerpt: Learn how to implement robust multi-language support in your web applications. This tutorial covers Laravel localization fundamentals, from managing language files and dynamic translation keys to optimizing user-specific locale switching for a global audience.
content:
If your app needs to support more than one language — for example, English and Arabic — Laravel's localization system makes this straightforward. This tutorial covers translation files, switching languages, and handling RTL (right-to-left) layouts.

Step 1: Create Language Files

Laravel organizes translations into folders by language code inside lang/:

lang/
├── en/
│   └── messages.php
└── ar/
    └── messages.php

lang/en/messages.php

return [
    'welcome' => 'Welcome to our store',
    'add_to_cart' => 'Add to Cart',
];

lang/ar/messages.php

return [
    'welcome' => 'مرحباً بكم في متجرنا',
    'add_to_cart' => 'أضف إلى السلة',
];

Step 2: Use Translations in Blade

<h1>{{ __('messages.welcome') }}</h1>
<button>{{ __('messages.add_to_cart') }}</button>

Step 3: Setting the Default Language

In .env:

APP_LOCALE=en
APP_FALLBACK_LOCALE=en

Step 4: Switching Languages at Runtime

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;

App::setLocale('ar');

A common pattern is a middleware that sets the locale based on the URL or session:

php artisan make:middleware SetLocale

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Session;

class SetLocale
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next)
    {
        $locale = Session::get('locale', config('app.locale'));
        App::setLocale($locale);

        return $next($request);
    }
}

A Language Switcher

<a href="{{ route('locale.switch', 'en') }}">English</a>
<a href="{{ route('locale.switch', 'ar') }}">العربية</a>

Route::get('/locale/{locale}', function ($locale) {
    session(['locale' => $locale]);
    return redirect()->back();
})->name('locale.switch');

Translation Strings With Variables

// lang/en/messages.php
'items_in_cart' => 'You have :count items in your cart',

{{ __('messages.items_in_cart', ['count' => 3]) }}

Pluralization

'apples' => 'There is one apple|There are :count apples',

{{ trans_choice('messages.apples', $count) }}

Handling RTL Layouts (for Arabic and Other RTL Languages)

Set the dir and lang attributes dynamically on your layout:

<html lang="{{ app()->getLocale() }}" dir="{{ app()->getLocale() === 'ar' ? 'rtl' : 'ltr' }}">

If you're using Tailwind CSS, load an RTL-aware plugin or maintain separate rtl: utility overrides, since spacing, margins, and text alignment often need to be mirrored (e.g., ml-4 in LTR should become mr-4 in RTL).

Validation Messages in Multiple Languages

Laravel automatically translates built-in validation messages if a lang/{locale}/validation.php file exists. You can publish the default language files to customize them:

php artisan lang:publish

Structuring Larger Translation Files

For bigger apps, split translations into logical files instead of one giant messages.php:

lang/en/
├── auth.php
├── products.php
├── validation.php

{{ __('products.add_to_cart') }}

title: Laravel Caching Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Master Laravel caching to significantly boost your application performance. This beginner-friendly guide explores cache drivers like Redis and File, essential methods, and practical code examples to optimize database queries effectively.
content:
Some data doesn't change often but is expensive to fetch — a list of categories, site-wide settings, or the results of a slow database query. Instead of recalculating it on every request, you can store it in a cache and reuse it instantly.

Configuring a Cache Driver

In .env:

CACHE_STORE=database

Other common options: file, redis, memcached. database or file are perfectly fine starting points; redis is the standard choice once performance really matters.

If using the database driver:

php artisan cache:table
php artisan migrate

Storing Data in the Cache

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;

Cache::put('site_settings', $settings, 3600); // cached for 3600 seconds (1 hour)

Retrieving Cached Data

$settings = Cache::get('site_settings');

// With a fallback default if not cached
$settings = Cache::get('site_settings', []);

The remember() Method (Most Commonly Used)

This is the pattern you'll use constantly: check the cache, and if it's empty, run the query and cache the result automatically.

$categories = Cache::remember('categories', 3600, function () {
    return Category::all();
});

First call: runs the query and caches it. Every call after that (within the hour): returns the cached result instantly, with zero database queries.

Caching Forever

Cache::forever('app_version', '2.1.0');

Checking If a Key Exists

if (Cache::has('site_settings')) {
    // ...
}

Removing Cached Data

Cache::forget('site_settings');

Clear everything:

Cache::flush();

Or via Artisan:

php artisan cache:clear

A Real Example: Caching an Expensive Query

public function index()
{
    $topProducts = Cache::remember('top_products', 1800, function () {
        return Product::orderBy('sales_count', 'desc')->take(10)->get();
    });

    return view('products.top', compact('topProducts'));
}

Clearing the Cache When Data Changes

Cached data can go stale. Whenever the underlying data changes, clear the relevant cache key:

public function update(Request $request, Product $product)
{
    $product->update($request->validated());

    Cache::forget('top_products');

    return redirect()->route('products.index');
}

Caching With Tags (Redis/Memcached Only)

Tags let you group related cache entries and clear them all at once:

Cache::tags(['products'])->put('featured', $featuredProducts, 3600);

// Clear everything tagged 'products'
Cache::tags(['products'])->flush();

Note: cache tags are NOT supported by the database or file drivers — only Redis and Memcached.

What Should You Cache?

Good to Cache Avoid Caching Site settings/configuration Data that changes every request Category/navigation lists User-specific, frequently changing data Expensive report calculations Anything requiring real-time accuracy (e.g., stock counts at checkout) API responses from external services Sensitive data without proper access checks

What's Next?

If your app serves users in different countries or languages, you'll want to adapt your content accordingly. Let's cover Laravel's localization system next.

title: Laravel Notifications Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Master Laravel Notifications with this comprehensive beginner's guide. Learn how to send real-time alerts via email, SMS, and Slack, leveraging built-in notification channels to streamline user communication in your web applications.
content:
Notifications let you alert users through multiple channels — email, database (for in-app alerts), SMS, Slack — all using the same simple, unified syntax. This is different from the Mail system you learned earlier: Notifications are more flexible and can target multiple channels at once.

Step 1: Create a Notification

php artisan make:notification InvoicePaid

This creates app/Notifications/InvoicePaid.php.

Step 2: Define the Notification

namespace App\Notifications;

use App\Models\Invoice;
use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Notifications\Notification;
use Illuminate\Notifications\Messages\MailMessage;

class InvoicePaid extends Notification
{
    use Queueable;

    public function __construct(public Invoice $invoice) {}

    public function via($notifiable): array
    {
        return ['mail', 'database'];
    }

    public function toMail($notifiable): MailMessage
    {
        return (new MailMessage)
            ->subject('Invoice Paid')
            ->line("Invoice #{$this->invoice->id} has been paid.")
            ->action('View Invoice', url('/invoices/' . $this->invoice->id))
            ->line('Thank you for your business!');
    }

    public function toArray($notifiable): array
    {
        return [
            'invoice_id' => $this->invoice->id,
            'amount' => $this->invoice->amount,
        ];
    }
}

  • via() defines which channels to use

  • toMail() defines the email content

  • toArray() defines what gets stored for the database channel

Step 3: Set Up the Database Channel

php artisan notifications:table
php artisan migrate

Step 4: Add the Notifiable Trait to Your User Model

This is already included by default on the User model:

use Illuminate\Notifications\Notifiable;

class User extends Authenticatable
{
    use Notifiable;
}

Step 5: Send the Notification

use App\Notifications\InvoicePaid;

$user->notify(new InvoicePaid($invoice));

That's it — Laravel sends it through every channel defined in via().

Displaying Database Notifications in Blade

@foreach (auth()->user()->unreadNotifications as $notification)
    <p>Invoice #{{ $notification->data['invoice_id'] }} paid: ${{ $notification->data['amount'] }}</p>
@endforeach

Marking Notifications as Read

$notification = auth()->user()->unreadNotifications()->find($id);
$notification->markAsRead();

Mark all as read:

auth()->user()->unreadNotifications->markAsRead();

Counting Unread Notifications (For a Bell Icon Badge)

<span class="badge">{{ auth()->user()->unreadNotifications->count() }}</span>

Queueing Notifications

Since the Queueable trait is already included, you can push notifications to the background just like jobs:

class InvoicePaid extends Notification implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Queueable;
}

Notifications vs Mailables: Which to Use?

Use Mailables When... Use Notifications When... You're only ever sending email You need multiple channels (email + database + SMS) No in-app notification tracking needed You want a notification bell / activity feed Simple, one-off transactional emails Reusable alerts tied to specific events (order shipped, comment received, etc.)

What's Next?

Notifications and page loads both benefit from not repeating expensive work. Let's look at how caching can speed up your Laravel app significantly.

Next step: Laravel Caching Tutorial for Beginners

title: Laravel Sessions and Cookies Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Master state management in Laravel by understanding the critical differences between sessions and cookies. This guide covers practical implementations, from configuring session drivers and handling flash data to managing persistent cookies for a seamless user experience.
content:
HTTP is stateless — every request is independent and forgets everything from the last one. Sessions and cookies let your app "remember" information about a user between requests, like login status, cart contents, or temporary success messages.

What's the Difference Between a Session and a Cookie?

  • Cookies are small pieces of data stored in the user's browser and sent with every request.

  • Sessions store data on the server (or in a fast storage layer like Redis/database), with only a session ID stored in a cookie to identify which user's data to load.

Sessions are generally more secure since the actual data never leaves the server.

Configuring the Session Driver

In .env:

SESSION_DRIVER=database

Other common options: file, cookie, redis. database is a solid, simple default for most apps.

If using the database driver, create the sessions table:

php artisan session:table
php artisan migrate

Storing Data in the Session

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Session;

Session::put('cart_total', 49.99);

Or using the request helper:

$request->session()->put('cart_total', 49.99);

Retrieving Session Data

$total = Session::get('cart_total');

// With a default fallback value
$total = Session::get('cart_total', 0);

Checking If a Key Exists

if (Session::has('cart_total')) {
    // ...
}

Removing Session Data

Session::forget('cart_total');
Session::flush(); // clears everything

Flash Data (One-Time Messages)

Flash data is available for the next request only — perfect for "Saved successfully!" messages after a redirect.

public function store(Request $request)
{
    Task::create($request->all());

    return redirect()->route('tasks.index')->with('success', 'Task created!');
}

@if (session('success'))
    <div class="alert">{{ session('success') }}</div>
@endif

After that one page load, the message automatically disappears.

Working With Cookies

Setting a Cookie

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cookie;

return redirect('/dashboard')->withCookie(Cookie::make('theme', 'dark', 60));

The third argument (60) is the cookie's lifetime in minutes.

Reading a Cookie

$theme = $request->cookie('theme');

Creating a "Forever" Cookie

Cookie::forever('theme', 'dark');

Deleting a Cookie

return redirect('/dashboard')->withoutCookie('theme');

Practical Example: A Shopping Cart Using Sessions

public function add(Request $request, Product $product)
{
    $cart = Session::get('cart', []);
    $cart[$product->id] = [
        'name' => $product->name,
        'price' => $product->price,
        'quantity' => ($cart[$product->id]['quantity'] ?? 0) + 1,
    ];

    Session::put('cart', $cart);

    return redirect()->back()->with('success', 'Added to cart!');
}

When to Use Sessions vs Cookies vs Database

Use Case Best Option Login state Session (handled automatically by Laravel auth) One-time flash messages Session Simple, low-security preferences (theme, language) Cookie Data that must survive across devices/browsers Database (tied to the user account)

title: Laravel Collections Tutorial: Working With Arrays the Easy Way
excerpt: Master Laravel Collections to simplify array manipulation. Learn how to filter, transform, and aggregate data efficiently using fluent method chaining, and discover when to use Collection methods versus database-level filtering for optimal performance.
content:
Every time you run Model::all() or Model::get(), Laravel doesn't return a plain PHP array — it returns a Collection. Collections wrap arrays with dozens of convenient, readable methods for filtering, transforming, and analyzing data.

Creating a Collection

use Illuminate\Support\Collection;

$collection = collect([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);

Eloquent results are already collections automatically:

$products = Product::all(); // this is a Collection

Filtering Data

$expensive = $products->filter(function ($product) {
    return $product->price > 100;
});

Transforming Data With map

$names = $products->map(function ($product) {
    return strtoupper($product->name);
});

Extracting a Single Column With pluck

$names = $products->pluck('name');

Sorting

$sorted = $products->sortBy('price');
$sortedDesc = $products->sortByDesc('price');

Grouping Data

$grouped = $products->groupBy('category_id');

Summing, Averaging, and Counting

$total = $products->sum('price');
$average = $products->avg('price');
$count = $products->count();
$highest = $products->max('price');
$lowest = $products->min('price');

Checking If Any/All Items Match a Condition

$hasExpensiveItem = $products->contains(function ($product) {
    return $product->price > 1000;
});

$allInStock = $products->every(function ($product) {
    return $product->stock > 0;
});

Chaining Methods Together

This is where Collections really shine — you can chain multiple operations fluently:

$topProducts = $products
    ->filter(fn ($product) => $product->is_active)
    ->sortByDesc('price')
    ->take(5)
    ->pluck('name');

This reads almost like a sentence: filter active products, sort by price descending, take the top 5, and get just their names.

Converting a Collection Back to an Array

$array = $products->toArray();

Useful Collection Methods Cheat Sheet

Method Purpose ->filter() Keep items matching a condition ->map() Transform each item ->pluck('field') Extract a single column ->sortBy() / ->sortByDesc() Sort ascending/descending ->groupBy() Group items by a field ->sum() / ->avg() / ->count() Aggregate calculations ->first() / ->last() Get the first or last item ->unique() Remove duplicates ->chunk(10) Split into smaller groups ->each() Loop through and perform an action

Collections vs Query Builder: When to Filter Where

A common beginner mistake is fetching all records, then filtering with Collections in PHP:

// Inefficient — loads everything into memory first
$expensive = Product::all()->filter(fn ($p) => $p->price > 100);

Whenever possible, filter at the database level instead — it's far more efficient:

// Efficient — filtering happens in the database
$expensive = Product::where('price', '>', 100)->get();

Use Collection methods for logic that's difficult or impossible to express in SQL, or for working with data you've already retrieved.

title: Laravel Accessors, Mutators, and Query Scopes Explained
excerpt: Master Laravel Eloquent by leveraging accessors, mutators, and query scopes. Learn how to centralize data formatting, normalize input, and build reusable query logic to keep your models clean, maintainable, and efficient.
content:
As your models grow, you'll want to format data consistently and avoid repeating the same query conditions everywhere. Accessors, mutators, and query scopes solve exactly this — keeping formatting and query logic inside the model, where it belongs.

Accessors: Formatting Data When You Read It

An accessor transforms an attribute's value automatically whenever you access it.

namespace App\Models;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Casts\Attribute;

class Product extends Model
{
    protected function price(): Attribute
    {
        return Attribute::make(
            get: fn ($value) => '$' . number_format($value, 2),
        );
    }
}

Now, anywhere you access $product->price, it's automatically formatted:

echo $product->price; // "$25.99" instead of "25.99"

Mutators: Formatting Data Before It's Saved

A mutator transforms a value automatically before it's stored in the database.

protected function name(): Attribute
{
    return Attribute::make(
        set: fn ($value) => ucfirst($value),
    );
}

Product::create(['name' => 'wireless mouse']);
// Saved in the database as "Wireless mouse"

Combining Both (Get and Set)

protected function email(): Attribute
{
    return Attribute::make(
        get: fn ($value) => strtolower($value),
        set: fn ($value) => strtolower($value),
    );
}

Creating a Computed (Virtual) Attribute

Accessors can also build entirely new "virtual" attributes that don't exist as real database columns:

protected function fullName(): Attribute
{
    return Attribute::make(
        get: fn () => "{$this->first_name} {$this->last_name}",
    );
}

echo $user->full_name; // "Kareem Hassan"

Query Scopes: Reusable Query Conditions

Scopes let you package up common where conditions into reusable, readable methods.

Local Scopes

namespace App\Models;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Builder;

class Product extends Model
{
    public function scopeActive(Builder $query): void
    {
        $query->where('is_active', true);
    }

    public function scopePriceAbove(Builder $query, float $price): void
    {
        $query->where('price', '>', $price);
    }
}

Usage — call it without the scope prefix:

$products = Product::active()->get();

$products = Product::active()->priceAbove(50)->get();

Much more readable than repeating ->where('is_active', true) in every controller.

Global Scopes

A global scope applies automatically to every query on a model — useful for things like multi-tenancy or always excluding certain records.

namespace App\Models\Scopes;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Builder;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Scope;

class ActiveScope implements Scope
{
    public function apply(Builder $builder, Model $model): void
    {
        $builder->where('is_active', true);
    }
}

protected static function booted(): void
{
    static::addGlobalScope(new ActiveScope);
}

Now Product::all() automatically only returns active products, everywhere in your app, without needing to remember to add the condition manually.

When to Use Each

Feature Use It For Accessor Formatting output (currency, dates, capitalization) Mutator Cleaning/normalizing input before saving Local Scope Reusable, optional query filters Global Scope Rules that should ALWAYS apply to a model's queries

title: Laravel Soft Deletes Tutorial: Safely Removing Records
excerpt: Learn how to implement Laravel soft deletes to prevent accidental data loss. This comprehensive guide covers adding the deleted_at column, configuring your Eloquent models, and managing record restoration, forced deletions, and relationship handling.
content:
Permanently deleting data is risky — what if a user accidentally deletes an important record? Laravel's soft delete feature marks records as deleted without actually removing them from the database, so they can be restored later.

How Soft Deletes Work

Instead of removing a row, Laravel sets a deleted_at timestamp on it. Any record with a non-null deleted_at is automatically excluded from normal queries — but the data still exists.

Step 1: Add the deleted_at Column

php artisan make:migration add_soft_deletes_to_products_table --table=products

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schema;
use Illuminate\Database\Schema\Blueprint;

public function up(): void
{
    Schema::table('products', function (Blueprint $table) {
        $table->softDeletes();
    });
}

public function down(): void
{
    Schema::table('products', function (Blueprint $table) {
        $table->dropSoftDeletes();
    });
}

php artisan migrate

Step 2: Add the Trait to Your Model

namespace App\Models;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\SoftDeletes;

class Product extends Model
{
    use SoftDeletes;
}

Deleting a Record (Now Soft-Deletes Automatically)

$product = Product::find(1);
$product->delete();

This sets deleted_at instead of removing the row. Normal queries like Product::all() will no longer include it.

Restoring a Soft-Deleted Record

$product = Product::withTrashed()->find(1);
$product->restore();

Querying Soft-Deleted Records

// Include trashed records along with normal ones
Product::withTrashed()->get();

// Only trashed records
Product::onlyTrashed()->get();

Permanently Deleting a Record

If you truly need to remove a record forever:

$product = Product::withTrashed()->find(1);
$product->forceDelete();

Checking If a Record Is Soft-Deleted

if ($product->trashed()) {
    // it's been soft-deleted
}

Soft Deletes and Relationships

If a parent record is soft-deleted, related records aren't automatically soft-deleted with it — you handle that explicitly if needed:

protected static function boot()
{
    parent::boot();

    static::deleting(function ($product) {
        $product->reviews()->delete();
    });
}

Building a "Trash" / "Recently Deleted" Page

public function trashed()
{
    $products = Product::onlyTrashed()->paginate(10);
    return view('products.trashed', compact('products'));
}

@foreach ($products as $product)
    <p>{{ $product->name }}</p>
    <form action="{{ route('products.restore', $product->id) }}" method="POST">
        @csrf
        <button type="submit">Restore</button>
    </form>
@endforeach

public function restore($id)
{
    Product::withTrashed()->findOrFail($id)->restore();
    return redirect()->back();
}

When to Use Soft Deletes

  • User-generated content (posts, comments) where accidental deletion is common

  • Financial or order records that need to be recoverable/auditable

  • Anything where "undo" is an important feature

When NOT to Use Them

  • Extremely high-volume tables where the extra deleted_at index adds unnecessary overhead

  • Data with strict legal requirements to be permanently erased (e.g., certain privacy regulations)

title: Laravel Search Tutorial: Building a Simple Search Feature
excerpt: Learn how to implement robust search functionality in Laravel using the query builder. This tutorial covers building search forms, filtering across multiple columns, handling related data, and managing pagination, while providing tips on when to scale up to Laravel Scout.
content:
Almost every list of data — products, users, blog posts — eventually needs a search box. This tutorial covers building a simple, effective search feature using Laravel's query builder.

Step 1: Build the Search Form

<form method="GET" action="{{ route('products.index') }}">
    <input type="text" name="search" value="{{ request('search') }}" placeholder="Search products...">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

Using GET (not POST) keeps the search term visible in the URL — useful for sharing links and browser back/forward navigation.

Step 2: Filter Results in the Controller

public function index(Request $request)
{
    $search = $request->input('search');

    $products = Product::when($search, function ($query, $search) {
            $query->where('name', 'like', "%{$search}%");
        })
        ->paginate(10);

    return view('products.index', compact('products'));
}

when() only applies the where clause if a search term was actually provided — no need for a manual if statement.

Searching Multiple Columns

$products = Product::when($search, function ($query, $search) {
        $query->where('name', 'like', "%{$search}%")
              ->orWhere('description', 'like', "%{$search}%");
    })
    ->paginate(10);

Combining Search With Other Filters

public function index(Request $request)
{
    $products = Product::when($request->search, function ($query, $search) {
            $query->where('name', 'like', "%{$search}%");
        })
        ->when($request->category, function ($query, $category) {
            $query->where('category_id', $category);
        })
        ->when($request->sort, function ($query, $sort) {
            $query->orderBy('price', $sort === 'price_desc' ? 'desc' : 'asc');
        })
        ->paginate(10);

    return view('products.index', compact('products'));
}

Preserving Filters Across Pagination

{{ $products->appends(request()->query())->links() }}

Searching Related Data

To search products by their category name (a related table):

$products = Product::whereHas('category', function ($query) use ($search) {
        $query->where('name', 'like', "%{$search}%");
    })
    ->paginate(10);

A Note on Performance

LIKE '%search%' queries can become slow on very large tables because they can't use standard indexes efficiently. For small-to-medium apps this is perfectly fine. If you eventually need faster, more advanced search (fuzzy matching, relevance ranking), consider a dedicated search package like Laravel Scout paired with a search engine such as Meilisearch or Algolia.

Basic Laravel Scout Example (For Reference)

composer require laravel/scout

use Laravel\Scout\Searchable;

class Product extends Model
{
    use Searchable;
}

$products = Product::search($request->search)->paginate(10);

Scout is worth exploring once your search needs outgrow simple LIKE queries.

title: Laravel Pagination Tutorial: Splitting Data Into Pages
excerpt: Learn how to efficiently manage large datasets in Laravel using built-in pagination methods. This guide covers basic implementation, simple pagination, cursor-based performance optimization, and how to preserve query parameters for a seamless user experience.
content:
Loading thousands of database records onto a single page is slow and overwhelming for users. Laravel's built-in pagination makes it simple to split results into manageable pages.

Basic Pagination

public function index()
{
    $products = Product::paginate(10);

    return view('products.index', compact('products'));
}

paginate(10) returns 10 records per page and automatically detects the current page from the URL (?page=2).

Displaying Pagination Links in Blade

@foreach ($products as $product)
    <p>{{ $product->name }}</p>
@endforeach

{{ $products->links() }}

{{ $products->links() }} automatically renders "Previous/Next" and numbered page links, styled to match your CSS framework (Tailwind by default).

Simple Pagination (Previous/Next Only)

If you don't need numbered page links, this is more efficient for very large datasets:

$products = Product::simplePaginate(10);

Pagination With Conditions

$products = Product::where('is_active', true)
    ->orderBy('created_at', 'desc')
    ->paginate(10);

Preserving Query Strings (e.g., Filters)

If your page has search or filter parameters, preserve them across pages:

{{ $products->appends(request()->query())->links() }}

Customizing the Pagination View

Publish Laravel's default pagination views to customize their HTML:

php artisan vendor:publish --tag=laravel-pagination

Or specify a different view directly:

{{ $products->links('vendor.pagination.custom') }}

Accessing Pagination Metadata

<p>Showing {{ $products->firstItem() }} to {{ $products->lastItem() }} of {{ $products->total() }} results</p>

Method Returns ->total() Total number of records ->currentPage() The current page number ->lastPage() The last page number ->perPage() Items shown per page ->hasMorePages() Boolean — is there a next page?

Pagination in a JSON API

Returning a paginated Eloquent result from an API route automatically includes pagination metadata in the JSON response:

public function index()
{
    return Product::paginate(10);
}

Response:

{
    "data": [...],
    "current_page": 1,
    "last_page": 5,
    "per_page": 10,
    "total": 47
}

Cursor Pagination (For Very Large Datasets)

For huge tables where performance matters more than jumping to a specific page number, use cursor pagination:

$products = Product::orderBy('id')->cursorPaginate(10);

This is faster than standard pagination for large datasets since it avoids expensive OFFSET queries.

What's Next?

Once you're displaying paginated lists, users will often want to search and filter that data. Let's cover building search functionality next.

title: Laravel Deployment Guide: Taking Your App Live
excerpt: Ready to launch your Laravel application? This comprehensive guide walks you through essential deployment steps, from server configuration and environment setup to production-grade optimizations and a critical pre-launch security checklist.
content:
You've built your Laravel app locally — now it's time to put it on the internet. This guide covers the essential steps and a pre-launch checklist for deploying safely.

Hosting Options for Beginners

Option Best For Laravel Forge Managing your own VPS (DigitalOcean, AWS, etc.) with ease Laravel Cloud Fully managed Laravel-specific hosting Shared hosting (with SSH/Composer support) Budget-friendly, simple projects VPS (manual setup) Full control, more configuration required

For beginners, Forge or a managed platform removes most of the server-configuration headache.

Server Requirements

  • PHP 8.2+

  • Required PHP extensions: BCMath, Ctype, Fileinfo, JSON, Mbstring, OpenSSL, PDO, Tokenizer, XML

  • Composer

  • A web server (Nginx or Apache)

  • MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQLite

Step 1: Push Your Code

Use Git to push your project to your server (or connect your hosting platform directly to your GitHub repository).

git clone https://github.com/yourusername/your-app.git

Step 2: Install Dependencies

composer install --optimize-autoloader --no-dev

--no-dev skips development-only packages, keeping production lean.

Step 3: Set Up Your .env File

Never commit .env to Git. Instead, create it manually on the server:

cp .env.example .env
php artisan key:generate

Update it with production values:

APP_ENV=production
APP_DEBUG=false
APP_URL=https://yourdomain.com

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_DATABASE=your_production_db
DB_USERNAME=your_db_user
DB_PASSWORD=your_secure_password

Critical: APP_DEBUG must always be false in production — leaving it true exposes sensitive error details, including database credentials, to anyone who triggers an error.

Step 4: Run Migrations

php artisan migrate --force

--force is required to run migrations in a production environment without an interactive confirmation prompt.

Step 5: Set Correct File Permissions

The web server needs write access to specific folders:

chmod -R 775 storage bootstrap/cache
chown -R www-data:www-data storage bootstrap/cache

(Adjust the user/group depending on your server setup.)

Step 6: Build Frontend Assets

npm install
npm run build

Step 7: Optimize Laravel for Production

php artisan config:cache
php artisan route:cache
php artisan view:cache
php artisan event:cache

These commands cache your config, routes, views, and events so Laravel doesn't have to rebuild them on every single request — a significant performance boost.

Important: If you cache config with config:cache, remember to run php artisan config:clear before making further .env changes, otherwise old cached values will keep being used.

Point Your Web Server to public/

Your web server's document root must point to the project's public/ folder — never the project root. This keeps your .env, app/, and other sensitive files outside of what's publicly accessible.

Setting Up HTTPS

Use a free SSL certificate via Let's Encrypt (most managed platforms, including Forge, handle this automatically).

Pre-Launch Checklist

  • [ ] APP_ENV=production and APP_DEBUG=false

  • [ ] Real database credentials configured

  • [ ] .env file is NOT committed to Git

  • [ ] php artisan migrate --force has been run

  • [ ] Storage symlink created: php artisan storage:link

  • [ ] Config/routes/views cached

  • [ ] SSL certificate installed (HTTPS enabled)

  • [ ] Queue worker running via Supervisor (if using queues)

  • [ ] Scheduler cron entry added (if using task scheduling)

  • [ ] Error monitoring set up (e.g., logging, Sentry, or similar)

What's Next?

You've now covered the entire beginner-to-launch journey. From here, you're ready to explore more advanced topics like Laravel Livewire, advanced Eloquent relationships, and building larger-scale applications.

title: Laravel Testing Tutorial: Getting Started with PHPUnit and Pest
excerpt: Master the fundamentals of automated testing in Laravel. This guide walks you through setting up PHPUnit and Pest, demonstrating how to write robust feature and unit tests to ensure your application's reliability and maintainability.
content:
Manually clicking through every page after each change doesn't scale. Automated tests let you verify your application works correctly in seconds, every time you make a change. Laravel ships with excellent testing support built in.

PHPUnit vs Pest

Laravel supports two testing frameworks out of the box:

  • PHPUnit – the traditional, class-based testing framework

  • Pest – a newer, more readable syntax built on top of PHPUnit

Both work identically under the hood — Pest is just friendlier for beginners. New Laravel projects let you choose during installation.

Types of Tests

  • Unit tests – test a single piece of logic in isolation (e.g., a method on a class)

  • Feature tests – test a full HTTP request/response cycle (e.g., visiting a route, submitting a form)

As a beginner, you'll write mostly feature tests.

Creating a Test

php artisan make:test ProductTest

This creates tests/Feature/ProductTest.php.

A Basic Feature Test (PHPUnit style)

namespace Tests\Feature;

use Tests\TestCase;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Testing\RefreshDatabase;

class ProductTest extends TestCase
{
    use RefreshDatabase;

    public function test_products_page_loads_successfully(): void
    {
        $response = $this->get('/products');

        $response->assertStatus(200);
    }
}

RefreshDatabase resets your test database before each test, so tests never interfere with each other.

The Same Test in Pest

use App\Models\Product;

it('loads the products page successfully', function () {
    $response = $this->get('/products');

    $response->assertStatus(200);
});

Testing Database Interactions

public function test_a_product_can_be_created(): void
{
    $response = $this->post('/products', [
        'name' => 'Wireless Mouse',
        'price' => 25.99,
    ]);

    $response->assertRedirect('/products');

    $this->assertDatabaseHas('products', [
        'name' => 'Wireless Mouse',
    ]);
}

Testing Authenticated Routes

use App\Models\User;

public function test_authenticated_user_can_view_dashboard(): void
{
    $user = User::factory()->create();

    $response = $this->actingAs($user)->get('/dashboard');

    $response->assertStatus(200);
}

User::factory()->create() uses Laravel's model factories to generate a fake user instantly.

Testing Validation Errors

public function test_product_requires_a_name(): void
{
    $response = $this->post('/products', ['price' => 10]);

    $response->assertSessionHasErrors('name');
}

Common Assertions Cheat Sheet

Assertion Checks assertStatus(200) HTTP status code assertRedirect('/path') Response redirects correctly assertSee('text') Page contains specific text assertDatabaseHas('table', [...]) A matching row exists assertDatabaseMissing('table', [...]) No matching row exists assertSessionHasErrors('field') Validation failed on a field

Running Your Tests
