php artisan test

Run a single test file:

php artisan test --filter=ProductTest

Using a Separate Testing Database

In phpunit.xml, Laravel is usually configured to use SQLite in-memory for speed:

<env name="DB_CONNECTION" value="sqlite"/>
<env name="DB_DATABASE" value=":memory:"/>

This keeps your real development database untouched while testing.

What's Next?

Testing gives you confidence in your code — the next natural step is deploying that tested code to a live server for the world to use.

title: Laravel Task Scheduling Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Learn how to master task scheduling in Laravel. This tutorial covers setting up a single cron entry, defining recurring tasks, scheduling custom Artisan commands, and implementing best practices like preventing overlapping runs and handling failures.
content:
Many apps need recurring tasks — sending a daily digest email, cleaning up old records, generating nightly reports. Instead of manually configuring a separate cron job for each task, Laravel lets you define all your scheduled tasks in code, using one single cron entry on your server.

Step 1: Set Up the Single Cron Entry

On your server, add just one cron job that runs every minute:

* * * * * cd /path-to-your-project && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1

Laravel checks this every minute and decides internally which scheduled tasks actually need to run.

Step 2: Define Scheduled Tasks

routes/console.php (Laravel 11+)

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::command('reports:daily')->dailyAt('08:00');

Or schedule a closure directly:

Schedule::call(function () {
    // cleanup logic
})->daily();

Common Scheduling Frequencies

Method Runs ->everyMinute() Every minute ->everyFiveMinutes() Every 5 minutes ->hourly() Once an hour ->daily() Once a day at midnight ->dailyAt('13:00') Once a day at a specific time ->weekly() Once a week ->monthly() Once a month

Scheduling a Custom Artisan Command

First, create the command:

php artisan make:command SendDailyReport

namespace App\Console\Commands;

use Illuminate\Console\Command;

class SendDailyReport extends Command
{
    protected $signature = 'reports:daily';
    protected $description = 'Send the daily summary report to admins';

    public function handle(): void
    {
        // your report logic here
        $this->info('Daily report sent!');
    }
}

Test it manually first:

php artisan reports:daily

Then schedule it:

Schedule::command('reports:daily')->dailyAt('08:00');

Preventing Overlapping Runs

If a task might occasionally take longer than its schedule interval, prevent it from running twice at once:

Schedule::command('reports:daily')->dailyAt('08:00')->withoutOverlapping();

Running Tasks Only in Production

Schedule::command('cleanup:temp-files')
    ->daily()
    ->environments(['production']);

Getting Notified of Failures

Schedule::command('reports:daily')
    ->dailyAt('08:00')
    ->emailOutputOnFailure('admin@example.com');

Testing the Scheduler Locally

You don't need to wait for real cron timing during development. Run this to simulate a scheduler tick:

php artisan schedule:run

Or use this to keep testing continuously without touching your system's actual crontab:

php artisan schedule:work

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake Fix Adding a separate cron entry per task Only one entry is needed — Laravel handles the rest Forgetting the cron entry entirely Nothing will run — verify it's active with crontab -l Testing only in production Use php artisan schedule:work locally first

What's Next?

Manually testing every feature by clicking through your app doesn't scale. Let's introduce automated testing, so you can catch bugs before your users do.

title: Laravel Queues Tutorial: Running Jobs in the Background
excerpt: Learn how to optimize your Laravel application by offloading time-consuming tasks like email processing and PDF generation to background workers. This guide covers the end-to-end process of configuring queue drivers, dispatching jobs, managing retries, and deploying persistent workers using Supervisor.
content:
Some tasks — sending emails, processing images, generating PDFs — take time. Making a user wait for these to finish before their page loads is a bad experience. Laravel Queues let you push slow tasks into the background so your app stays fast.

How Queues Work (The Big Picture)

  1. You dispatch a Job (a class describing the task)

  2. Laravel stores it in a queue (database, Redis, etc.)

  3. A separate queue worker process picks it up and runs it — independently of your web request

Step 1: Configure a Queue Driver

In .env:

QUEUE_CONNECTION=database

For the database driver, create the required table:

php artisan queue:table
php artisan migrate

(In production, most teams eventually move to redis for better performance — but database is perfectly fine to start.)

Step 2: Create a Job

php artisan make:job ProcessOrder

namespace App\Jobs;

use App\Models\Order;
use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Bus\Dispatchable;
use Illuminate\Queue\InteractsWithQueue;
use Illuminate\Queue\SerializesModels;

class ProcessOrder implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable, SerializesModels;

    public function __construct(public Order $order) {}

    public function handle(): void
    {
        // Slow logic here: generate invoice, call external API, etc.
        sleep(5);
        $this->order->update(['status' => 'processed']);
    }
}

Step 3: Dispatch the Job

use App\Jobs\ProcessOrder;

ProcessOrder::dispatch($order);

The controller returns a response immediately — the job runs separately.

Step 4: Run the Queue Worker

php artisan queue:work

This starts a process that continuously checks for and runs queued jobs. Keep this running while developing.

Delaying a Job

ProcessOrder::dispatch($order)->delay(now()->addMinutes(10));

Handling Failed Jobs

Create the failed jobs table:

php artisan queue:failed-table
php artisan migrate

View failed jobs:

php artisan queue:failed

Retry a specific failed job:

php artisan queue:retry {id}

Retry all failed jobs:

php artisan queue:retry all

Setting Retry Limits

class ProcessOrder implements ShouldQueue
{
    public $tries = 3;
    public $backoff = 30; // seconds between retries
}

Running Queue Workers in Production

Running php artisan queue:work manually isn't reliable long-term — if it crashes, jobs stop processing. In production, use a process manager like Supervisor to keep the worker running automatically.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake Fix Forgetting to run queue:work Jobs pile up but never actually run Not restarting the worker after code changes Run php artisan queue:restart after deploying Passing an entire Eloquent model without SerializesModels Include the SerializesModels trait (already default in generated jobs)

What's Next?

Now that you can process background tasks, let's look at how to keep your app running smoothly with scheduled, recurring tasks — like daily reports or database cleanups.

title: Laravel Events and Listeners Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Learn how to decouple your Laravel application logic by implementing the Events and Listeners pattern. This guide covers creating events, registering listeners, and utilizing queues to handle side effects like email notifications efficiently without bloating your controllers.
content:
As your app grows, a single action (like placing an order) often needs to trigger multiple side effects — sending an email, updating inventory, notifying an admin. Cramming all of that into one controller method gets messy fast. Laravel's Events and Listeners system solves this cleanly.

What Are Events and Listeners?

  • An Event represents something that happened (e.g., OrderShipped)

  • A Listener reacts to that event (e.g., SendShipmentEmail)

One event can have multiple listeners, and your controller doesn't need to know about any of them — it just fires the event.

Step 1: Create an Event

php artisan make:event OrderShipped

namespace App\Events;

use App\Models\Order;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Events\Dispatchable;

class OrderShipped
{
    use Dispatchable;

    public function __construct(public Order $order) {}
}

Step 2: Create a Listener

php artisan make:listener SendShipmentNotification --event=OrderShipped

namespace App\Listeners;

use App\Events\OrderShipped;
use App\Mail\OrderConfirmation;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Mail;

class SendShipmentNotification
{
    public function handle(OrderShipped $event): void
    {
        Mail::to($event->order->email)->send(new OrderConfirmation($event->order));
    }
}

Step 3: Register the Event-Listener Pair

In Laravel 11+, this is done automatically if you used --event above. You can also register manually in app/Providers/EventServiceProvider.php (older versions) or via Event::listen().

Step 4: Fire the Event

use App\Events\OrderShipped;

public function ship(Order $order)
{
    $order->update(['status' => 'shipped']);

    OrderShipped::dispatch($order);

    return redirect()->back();
}

Your controller stays clean — it doesn't know or care what happens after the event fires.

Adding Multiple Listeners to One Event

Event::listen(OrderShipped::class, SendShipmentNotification::class);
Event::listen(OrderShipped::class, UpdateInventory::class);
Event::listen(OrderShipped::class, NotifyAdmin::class);

All three run whenever OrderShipped::dispatch() is called — no changes needed to the controller.

Queueing Listeners (Run in the Background)

If a listener does something slow (like sending an email), implement ShouldQueue:

use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;

class SendShipmentNotification implements ShouldQueue
{
    public function handle(OrderShipped $event): void
    {
        // this now runs in the background via the queue
    }
}

Built-in Events You Might Already Be Using

Laravel fires events automatically for things like:

  • Illuminate\Auth\Events\Login

  • Illuminate\Auth\Events\Registered

You can hook your own listeners into these without touching Laravel's core authentication code.

When to Use Events vs. Just Calling a Method

Use Events When... Just Call a Method When... Multiple unrelated things need to happen Only one simple action follows You want to decouple your code The logic is tightly related and simple Other developers/packages may want to "hook in" later It's a one-off, internal-only action

What's Next?

Some listeners and jobs are slow — sending emails, processing images, generating reports. Instead of making users wait, you can push this work to a queue and process it in the background.

title: Laravel Mail Tutorial: Sending Emails for Beginners
excerpt: Master email integration in Laravel. This step-by-step guide covers configuring SMTP drivers, creating Mailable classes, leveraging Markdown templates, and implementing background queueing for scalable, professional application notifications.
content:
Sending emails — welcome messages, order confirmations, password resets — is a core feature of most web apps. This tutorial shows you how to set up and send emails in Laravel.

Step 1: Configure Your Mail Driver

In your .env file:

MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_HOST=smtp.mailtrap.io
MAIL_PORT=2525
MAIL_USERNAME=your_username
MAIL_PASSWORD=your_password
MAIL_ENCRYPTION=tls
MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS=hello@example.com
MAIL_FROM_NAME="${APP_NAME}"

For local development, use Mailtrap or Mailpit — they catch emails in a safe testing inbox instead of sending them to real addresses.

Step 2: Create a Mailable Class

php artisan make:mail OrderConfirmation

This creates app/Mail/OrderConfirmation.php.

Step 3: Build the Mailable

namespace App\Mail;

use App\Models\Order;
use Illuminate\Mail\Mailable;
use Illuminate\Queue\SerializesModels;

class OrderConfirmation extends Mailable
{
    use SerializesModels;

    public function __construct(public Order $order) {}

    public function build()
    {
        return $this->subject('Your Order Confirmation')
                    ->view('emails.order-confirmation')
                    ->with(['order' => $this->order]);
    }
}

Step 4: Create the Email Template

resources/views/emails/order-confirmation.blade.php

<h1>Thank you for your order, {{ $order->customer_name }}!</h1>
<p>Order #{{ $order->id }} — Total: ${{ $order->total }}</p>

Step 5: Send the Email

use App\Mail\OrderConfirmation;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Mail;

Mail::to($order->email)->send(new OrderConfirmation($order));

Sending to Multiple Recipients

Mail::to($order->email)
    ->cc('manager@example.com')
    ->bcc('records@example.com')
    ->send(new OrderConfirmation($order));

Queueing Emails (Recommended for Production)

Sending mail directly can slow down your app while it waits for the mail server. Queue it instead so it sends in the background:

Mail::to($order->email)->queue(new OrderConfirmation($order));

This requires a working queue driver — covered in a later article.

Using Markdown Mailables (Pre-Styled Emails)

php artisan make:mail OrderConfirmation --markdown=emails.order-confirmation

@component('mail::message')
# Order Confirmation

Thanks for your order, {{ $order->customer_name }}!

@component('mail::button', ['url' => $orderUrl])
View Order
@endcomponent

Thanks,<br>
{{ config('app.name') }}
@endcomponent

This gives you a professional, responsive email design with zero CSS work.

Testing Emails Without Sending Real Ones

Set your mail driver to log in .env:

MAIL_MAILER=log

Emails will be written to storage/logs/laravel.log instead of actually sending — perfect for local testing.

What's Next?

Sending a single email is simple — but real apps often need to react to events across multiple parts of the app (e.g., "when an order is placed, send an email AND update inventory AND notify the admin"). That's where Events and Listeners come in.

title: Laravel File Upload Tutorial: Images and Documents Made Easy
excerpt: Master file handling in Laravel with this comprehensive guide. Learn how to securely upload, validate, and store images and documents using Laravel's robust Storage facade and Request validation.
content:
Almost every real app needs file uploads — profile pictures, product images, documents. This tutorial covers uploading files in Laravel from start to finish.

Step 1: Create the Upload Form

<form action="{{ route('products.store') }}" method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    @csrf
    <input type="file" name="image">
    <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>

The enctype="multipart/form-data" attribute is required — without it, files won't be sent at all.

Step 2: Validate the Upload

$request->validate([
    'image' => 'required|image|mimes:jpg,jpeg,png|max:2048',
]);

  • image – must be a valid image file

  • mimes:jpg,jpeg,png – restrict allowed extensions

  • max:2048 – maximum size in kilobytes (2MB here)

Step 3: Store the File

public function store(Request $request)
{
    $request->validate([
        'image' => 'required|image|max:2048',
    ]);

    $path = $request->file('image')->store('products', 'public');

    Product::create([
        'name' => $request->name,
        'image' => $path,
    ]);

    return redirect()->route('products.index');
}

store('products', 'public') saves the file into storage/app/public/products and returns the relative path to save in your database.

Step 4: Create the Storage Symlink

Laravel keeps uploaded files outside the public folder for security, then symlinks a public/storage folder to it:

php artisan storage:link

Run this once per project — without it, uploaded files won't be accessible from the browser.

Step 5: Display the Uploaded Image

<img src="{{ asset('storage/' . $product->image) }}" alt="{{ $product->name }}">

Renaming Files on Upload

By default, Laravel generates a random filename. To use a custom name:

$file = $request->file('image');
$filename = time() . '_' . $file->getClientOriginalName();
$path = $file->storeAs('products', $filename, 'public');

Uploading Multiple Files

<input type="file" name="images[]" multiple>

foreach ($request->file('images') as $image) {
    $paths[] = $image->store('products', 'public');
}

Deleting an Uploaded File

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Storage;

Storage::disk('public')->delete($product->image);

Common Errors

Error Fix Image doesn't display Run php artisan storage:link "File too large" Check both Laravel's max: rule and upload_max_filesize in php.ini Form fields empty on submit Add enctype="multipart/form-data" to the form

What's Next?

Now that users can upload data, you'll often need to notify them by email — for example, confirming an order or a password reset. Let's cover Laravel's mail system next.

title: Common Laravel Beginner Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)
excerpt: Struggling with Laravel errors? From N+1 performance issues to mass assignment exceptions, we break down 12 common mistakes new Laravel developers make and provide actionable, clean-code solutions to help you build more robust applications.
content:
Every Laravel developer makes these mistakes when starting out. This article rounds up the most common ones, why they happen, and exactly how to fix them — so you can skip the frustration.

1. Forgetting $fillable (Mass Assignment Errors)

The problem:

Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\MassAssignmentException: Add [name] to fillable property

Why it happens: Laravel blocks mass assignment by default as a security measure.

The fix: Whitelist the fields you want to allow:

class Product extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = ['name', 'price', 'description'];
}

2. The N+1 Query Problem

The problem: Your page loads slowly because of hundreds of unnecessary database queries.

// Bad: runs 1 query, then 1 extra query PER post
$posts = Post::all();
foreach ($posts as $post) {
    echo $post->user->name;
}

The fix: Eager load relationships:

$posts = Post::with('user')->get();

3. Forgetting @csrf in Forms

The problem:

419 Page Expired

Why it happens: Laravel protects every POST/PUT/DELETE form against CSRF attacks and requires a token.

The fix: Always include it in your forms:

<form method="POST" action="/products">
    @csrf
</form>

4. Using GET Forms for PUT/DELETE Actions

The problem: HTML forms only natively support GET and POST — trying to delete a record doesn't work as expected.

The fix: Use Laravel's method spoofing:

<form method="POST" action="/products/1">
    @csrf
    @method('DELETE')
</form>

5. Not Running Migrations After Pulling New Code

The problem:

SQLSTATE[42S02]: Base table or view not found

The fix: Whenever you pull new code (or switch branches) that includes new migrations, run:

php artisan migrate

6. Editing Compiled/Cached Files Directly

The problem: Changes to routes, config, or views don't seem to take effect.

Why it happens: Laravel caches routes/config in production for performance — old cached versions are still being used.

The fix:

php artisan config:clear
php artisan route:clear
php artisan view:clear

7. Committing the .env File to Git

The problem: Database passwords, API keys, and secrets get exposed publicly.

The fix: Ensure .env is listed in .gitignore (it is by default in fresh Laravel installs — don't remove it). Use .env.example to share which variables are needed, without the actual secret values.

8. Not Validating User Input

The problem: Bad or malicious data makes it into your database.

The fix: Always validate incoming requests:

$request->validate([
    'email' => 'required|email',
]);

9. Querying Inside Blade Views

The problem:

@foreach (App\Models\Product::all() as $product)

Why it's bad: Mixes business logic with presentation, making code harder to test and maintain.

The fix: Fetch data in the controller and pass it to the view:

public function index()
{
    $products = Product::all();
    return view('products.index', compact('products'));
}

10. Not Using Route Model Binding

The problem: Manually looking up records in every controller method:

public function edit($id)
{
    $product = Product::findOrFail($id);
    return view('products.edit', compact('product'));
}

The fix: Let Laravel do it automatically:

public function edit(Product $product)
{
    return view('products.edit', compact('product'));
}

11. Ignoring the Laravel Log File

The problem: An error occurs with no obvious message on screen.

The fix: Check storage/logs/laravel.log — it contains detailed stack traces for almost every error in your app.

12. Not Understanding APP_DEBUG

The problem: Detailed error pages either don't show up locally, or (worse) show up in production, leaking sensitive information.

The fix: In your .env file:

APP_DEBUG=true   # local development only
APP_DEBUG=false  # always false in production

Final Thoughts

Every Laravel developer — no matter how experienced — has run into every mistake on this list at some point. Recognizing these patterns early will save you hours of debugging as you continue building. This wraps up the "Laravel Tutorial for Beginners" series — from installation all the way to APIs and common pitfalls.

title: Laravel API Tutorial: Build a REST API for Beginners
excerpt: Learn how to build a robust REST API with Laravel. This step-by-step guide covers setting up API routes, utilizing API resource controllers, formatting JSON responses, and implementing secure authentication with Laravel Sanctum.
content:
Not every Laravel app needs to render HTML pages. If you're building a mobile app backend or a JavaScript frontend (React, Vue), you'll want Laravel to serve data as JSON through a REST API. This tutorial walks through building one from scratch.

API Routes Live in a Separate File

Unlike web routes, API routes are automatically prefixed with /api and are stateless (no sessions/CSRF by default). Define them in routes/api.php.

Note: In newer Laravel versions, if routes/api.php doesn't exist yet, run: php artisan install:api

Step 1: Create the Model and Migration

php artisan make:model Product -m

Schema::create('products', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->string('name');
    $table->decimal('price', 8, 2);
    $table->timestamps();
});

php artisan migrate

Step 2: Create an API Resource Controller

php artisan make:controller Api/ProductController --api

The --api flag generates a controller with only the five methods relevant to APIs (no create/edit form methods, since there's no HTML involved).

Step 3: Define API Routes

routes/api.php

use App\Http\Controllers\Api\ProductController;

Route::apiResource('products', ProductController::class);

This automatically creates:

Method URL Action GET /api/products List all products POST /api/products Create a product GET /api/products/{id} Show one product PUT/PATCH /api/products/{id} Update a product DELETE /api/products/{id} Delete a product

Step 4: Build the Controller

namespace App\Http\Controllers\Api;

use App\Http\Controllers\Controller;
use App\Models\Product;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;

class ProductController extends Controller
{
    public function index()
    {
        return Product::all();
    }

    public function store(Request $request)
    {
        $validated = $request->validate([
            'name' => 'required|string|max:255',
            'price' => 'required|numeric|min:0',
        ]);

        $product = Product::create($validated);

        return response()->json($product, 201);
    }

    public function show(Product $product)
    {
        return $product;
    }

    public function update(Request $request, Product $product)
    {
        $validated = $request->validate([
            'name' => 'sometimes|string|max:255',
            'price' => 'sometimes|numeric|min:0',
        ]);

        $product->update($validated);

        return response()->json($product);
    }

    public function destroy(Product $product)
    {
        $product->delete();

        return response()->json(null, 204);
    }
}

Returning an Eloquent model or collection directly (like in index()) automatically converts it to JSON — Laravel handles that for you.

Testing the API

Use a tool like Postman, Insomnia, or curl:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/products

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Keyboard", "price": 49.99}'

Formatting Responses With API Resources

Raw models can expose fields you don't want to return. API Resources let you control the exact JSON shape:

php artisan make:resource ProductResource

class ProductResource extends JsonResource
{
    public function toArray($request): array
    {
        return [
            'id' => $this->id,
            'name' => $this->name,
            'price' => '$' . number_format($this->price, 2),
        ];
    }
}

Use it in your controller:

public function index()
{
    return ProductResource::collection(Product::all());
}

Authenticating Your API With Sanctum

For most beginner APIs, Laravel Sanctum is the standard choice for token-based authentication:

php artisan install:api

Protect routes:

Route::middleware('auth:sanctum')->group(function () {
    Route::apiResource('products', ProductController::class);
});

Clients authenticate by sending a bearer token in their request headers:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN_HERE

What's Next?

You've now covered the full core of Laravel — routing, Blade, controllers, Eloquent, auth, validation, middleware, Artisan, and APIs. To wrap up the series, let's look at the most common mistakes beginners make (and how to avoid them).

Next step: Common Laravel Beginner Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)

title: Laravel Artisan Commands Every Beginner Should Know
excerpt: Master Laravel's Artisan CLI with this comprehensive guide for beginners. Learn essential commands for project setup, database management, file generation, and optimization to streamline your development workflow.
content:
Artisan is Laravel's built-in command-line tool. It automates repetitive tasks so you don't have to create files or run maintenance tasks by hand. This cheat sheet covers the commands you'll reach for constantly as a beginner.

Viewing All Available Commands

php artisan list

Project Setup & Server

Command Purpose php artisan serve Start the local development server php artisan --version Check your installed Laravel version php artisan key:generate Generate a new application encryption key

File Generation ("make" Commands)

Command Creates php artisan make:controller ProductController A controller php artisan make:controller ProductController --resource A CRUD-ready controller php artisan make:model Product A model php artisan make:model Product -m A model + migration together php artisan make:migration create_products_table A migration file php artisan make:seeder ProductSeeder A database seeder php artisan make:factory ProductFactory A model factory (fake data) php artisan make:middleware CheckAge A middleware class php artisan make:request StoreProductRequest A form request class php artisan make:component Alert A Blade component php artisan make:rule NoBadWords A custom validation rule php artisan make:command SendReminders A custom Artisan command php artisan make:event OrderShipped An event class php artisan make:listener SendShipmentNotification An event listener php artisan make:notification InvoicePaid A notification class php artisan make:job ProcessPodcast A queueable job php artisan make:policy ProductPolicy An authorization policy

Database Commands

Command Purpose php artisan migrate Run all pending migrations php artisan migrate:rollback Undo the last batch of migrations php artisan migrate:fresh Drop all tables and re-migrate (dev only!) php artisan migrate:fresh --seed Fresh migrate + run seeders php artisan db:seed Run database seeders php artisan migrate:status Show which migrations have run

Routing

Command Purpose php artisan route:list Show all registered routes php artisan route:list --name=product Filter routes by name

Cache & Optimization

Command Purpose php artisan cache:clear Clear the application cache php artisan config:clear Clear cached config php artisan view:clear Clear compiled Blade views php artisan route:clear Clear cached routes php artisan optimize Cache config, routes, and events for production php artisan optimize:clear Clear all caches at once

Tinker (Interactive PHP Shell)

php artisan tinker

Lets you run PHP/Eloquent code directly against your app — great for quick testing:

>>> App\Models\Product::count()
>>> App\Models\Product::first()

Queues

Command Purpose php artisan queue:work Start processing queued jobs php artisan queue:failed List failed jobs php artisan queue:retry all Retry all failed jobs

A Beginner's Daily Workflow Example

php artisan make:model Order -m
php artisan migrate
php artisan make:controller OrderController --resource
php artisan route:list
php artisan serve

Pro Tip: Command Shortcuts

Most make: commands accept -m (migration), -f (factory), -s (seeder), and -c (controller) as shortcuts:

php artisan make:model Order -mfsc

This single command generates a model, migration, factory, seeder, and controller all at once.

What's Next?

You now have a solid command-line toolkit. In the next article, we'll shift from building pages to building a REST API — essential if you ever plan to build a mobile app or a decoupled frontend.

title: Laravel Middleware Tutorial: What It Is and How to Use It
excerpt: Master Laravel middleware with this comprehensive guide. Learn how to filter HTTP requests, secure your routes with custom authentication logic, and streamline your backend workflow using practical, step-by-step examples.
content:
Middleware acts as a filter for HTTP requests entering your application. It runs before (or after) a request reaches your controller, making it perfect for tasks like authentication checks, logging, or blocking certain users.

What is Middleware, Really?

Think of middleware as a series of checkpoints a request must pass through before reaching its final destination (your controller). Each checkpoint can:

  • Allow the request to continue

  • Modify the request

  • Reject the request entirely (e.g., redirect to login)

Built-in Middleware You've Already Used

Middleware Purpose auth Blocks access unless the user is logged in guest Blocks access if the user IS logged in (used on login/register pages) verified Requires a verified email address throttle Rate-limits requests (prevents abuse)

Example:

Route::get('/dashboard', function () {
    return view('dashboard');
})->middleware('auth');

Creating Custom Middleware

Let's build middleware that only allows admin users to access certain pages.

php artisan make:middleware EnsureUserIsAdmin

This creates app/Http/Middleware/EnsureUserIsAdmin.php:

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class EnsureUserIsAdmin
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        if (!$request->user() || !$request->user()->is_admin) {
            abort(403, 'Unauthorized');
        }

        return $next($request);
    }
}

  • $next($request) passes the request along to the next step (another middleware or the controller)

  • Calling abort(403) stops the request immediately

Registering Middleware

In Laravel 11+, register it inside bootstrap/app.php:

->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware) {
    $middleware->alias([
        'admin' => \App\Http\Middleware\EnsureUserIsAdmin::class,
    ]);
})

Applying Your Custom Middleware

Route::get('/admin/settings', function () {
    return 'Admin settings page';
})->middleware('admin');

Applying Multiple Middleware

Route::get('/admin/settings', function () {
    return 'Admin settings page';
})->middleware(['auth', 'admin']);

Laravel runs these in order — auth first, then admin.

Applying Middleware to a Group of Routes

Route::middleware(['auth', 'admin'])->group(function () {
    Route::get('/admin/dashboard', fn() => 'Dashboard');
    Route::get('/admin/users', fn() => 'Users');
});

Passing Parameters to Middleware

public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next, string $role): Response
{
    if ($request->user()->role !== $role) {
        abort(403);
    }

    return $next($request);
}

Route::get('/editor', fn() => 'Editor Panel')->middleware('role:editor');

Middleware That Runs After the Request

public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
{
    $response = $next($request);

    // Runs after the controller has responded
    $response->headers->set('X-Custom-Header', 'MyValue');

    return $response;
}

When to Use Middleware

  • Authentication and authorization checks

  • Logging requests

  • Rate limiting sensitive routes (e.g., login attempts)

  • Setting locale/language based on user preference

  • Checking for maintenance mode

What's Next?

You've now covered most of the core building blocks of Laravel. Let's speed up your workflow with Artisan — the command-line tool you've been using throughout this series, but haven't explored fully yet.

title: Laravel Form Validation Tutorial with Examples
excerpt: Master Laravel form validation with this comprehensive guide. Learn how to secure your applications using built-in validation rules, Form Request classes, custom validation logic, and efficient error handling in Blade templates.
content:
Validating user input is essential for keeping your application secure and your database clean. This tutorial covers how Laravel's validation system works, from basic rules to custom validation logic.

Basic Validation in a Controller

public function store(Request $request)
{
    $validated = $request->validate([
        'title' => 'required|max:255',
        'email' => 'required|email',
        'price' => 'required|numeric|min:0',
    ]);

    Product::create($validated);

    return redirect()->route('products.index');
}

If validation fails, Laravel automatically redirects the user back to the previous page with the errors and their old input — no extra code needed.

Displaying Validation Errors in Blade

<form action="{{ route('products.store') }}" method="POST">
    @csrf

    <input type="text" name="title" value="{{ old('title') }}">
    @error('title')
        <p style="color:red">{{ $message }}</p>
    @enderror

    <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

  • old('title') repopulates the field with the user's previous input

  • @error('title') displays the specific error message for that field

Showing All Errors at Once

@if ($errors->any())
    <ul>
        @foreach ($errors->all() as $error)
            <li>{{ $error }}</li>
        @endforeach
    </ul>
@endif

Common Validation Rules

Rule What It Checks required Field must not be empty email Must be a valid email format numeric Must be a number min:3 / max:255 Minimum/maximum length or value unique:users,email Must not already exist in the table confirmed Must match a _confirmation field (e.g., password) date Must be a valid date in:draft,published Must be one of the listed values image Must be an uploaded image file nullable Field is optional

Example: Registration Validation

$request->validate([
    'name' => 'required|string|max:255',
    'email' => 'required|email|unique:users,email',
    'password' => 'required|min:8|confirmed',
]);

This requires a matching password_confirmation field in the form.

Using Form Request Classes (Cleaner Approach)

For larger forms, move validation logic out of the controller into its own class:

php artisan make:request StoreProductRequest

app/Http/Requests/StoreProductRequest.php

class StoreProductRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function authorize(): bool
    {
        return true;
    }

    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'title' => 'required|max:255',
            'price' => 'required|numeric|min:0',
        ];
    }

    public function messages(): array
    {
        return [
            'title.required' => 'Please give your product a title.',
        ];
    }
}

Then simplify your controller:

use App\Http\Requests\StoreProductRequest;

public function store(StoreProductRequest $request)
{
    Product::create($request->validated());
    return redirect()->route('products.index');
}

Laravel automatically validates the request before the method body even runs.

Custom Validation Rules

For logic that doesn't fit built-in rules, create a custom rule:

php artisan make:rule NoBadWords

class NoBadWords implements Rule
{
    public function passes($attribute, $value): bool
    {
        return !str_contains(strtolower($value), 'spam');
    }

    public function message(): string
    {
        return 'The :attribute contains a banned word.';
    }
}

Usage:

$request->validate([
    'title' => ['required', new NoBadWords],
]);

Validating Arrays and Nested Data

$request->validate([
    'items' => 'required|array',
    'items.*.name' => 'required|string',
    'items.*.quantity' => 'required|integer|min:1',
]);

What's Next?

Validation protects individual routes, but you'll often need broader rules that run on every request — like checking if a user is authenticated or has permission. That's where middleware comes in.

title: Laravel Authentication Tutorial: Login & Register System
excerpt: Master Laravel authentication by leveraging Laravel Breeze to implement secure login, registration, and password management. This tutorial covers essential setup, route protection with middleware, and best practices for scoping data to authenticated users.
content:
Almost every real-world application needs user accounts. Laravel makes authentication easy with Laravel Breeze — an official starter kit that gives you login, registration, password reset, and email verification out of the box.

Why Use Breeze Instead of Building Auth From Scratch?

Building authentication manually means handling password hashing, session security, CSRF protection, and edge cases correctly — it's easy to get wrong. Breeze provides a secure, well-tested foundation you can customize.

Step 1: Install Breeze

composer require laravel/breeze --dev
php artisan breeze:install

You'll be prompted to choose a frontend stack (Blade, React, Vue, or API-only). For beginners, choose Blade.

Step 2: Install Frontend Dependencies

npm install
npm run dev

Step 3: Run Migrations

Breeze adds a users table migration automatically:

php artisan migrate

What Breeze Gives You

After installation, you automatically get these routes and views:

Feature Route Register /register Login /login Logout /logout Forgot password /forgot-password Reset password /reset-password Email verification /verify-email Profile update /profile

Protecting Routes With the auth Middleware

Now that authentication exists, you can restrict routes to logged-in users only:

Route::get('/dashboard', function () {
    return view('dashboard');
})->middleware('auth');

Unauthenticated users trying to access /dashboard will be redirected to /login.

Restricting an Entire Group of Routes

Route::middleware('auth')->group(function () {
    Route::resource('tasks', TaskController::class);
});

Getting the Currently Logged-In User

Anywhere in your app:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Auth;

$user = Auth::user();
echo $user->name;

Or, inside a Blade view:

@auth
    <p>Welcome back, {{ Auth::user()->name }}</p>
@else
    <a href="{{ route('login') }}">Login</a>
@endauth

Scoping Data to the Logged-In User

Going back to our Task Manager example from the previous article — you'll want each user to only see their own tasks.

1. Add a user_id column:

php artisan make:migration add_user_id_to_tasks_table --table=tasks

Schema::table('tasks', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->foreignId('user_id')->constrained()->onDelete('cascade');
});

2. Update the controller:

public function index()
{
    $tasks = Auth::user()->tasks; // requires a hasMany relationship on User
    return view('tasks.index', compact('tasks'));
}

public function store(Request $request)
{
    $request->validate(['title' => 'required|max:255']);

    Auth::user()->tasks()->create($request->all());

    return redirect()->route('tasks.index');
}

3. Define the relationship in app/Models/User.php:

public function tasks()
{
    return $this->hasMany(Task::class);
}

Logging Out

Breeze handles this automatically, but manually it looks like:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Auth;

Auth::logout();

Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Forgetting to run npm run dev after installing Breeze (styles won't load)

  • Not applying the auth middleware, leaving pages publicly accessible

  • Querying all records instead of scoping by the logged-in user

What's Next?

Authentication is only useful if the data users submit is actually valid. Next, we'll dive deeper into Laravel's validation system.

Next step: Laravel Form Validation Tutorial with Examples

title: Laravel CRUD Tutorial: Build Your First App (Step-by-Step)
excerpt: Master the fundamentals of Laravel by building a robust Task Manager application. This step-by-step tutorial covers essential CRUD operations, including migrations, resource controllers, route model binding, and Blade templating, providing a solid foundation for your backend development journey.
content:
This tutorial brings together everything from earlier in the series — routing, controllers, migrations, Eloquent, and Blade — to build a complete CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) application: a simple Task Manager.

Step 1: Create the Model and Migration

php artisan make:model Task -m

Edit the migration file in database/migrations/:

public function up(): void
{
    Schema::create('tasks', function (Blueprint $table) {
        $table->id();
        $table->string('title');
        $table->text('description')->nullable();
        $table->boolean('is_completed')->default(false);
        $table->timestamps();
    });
}

Run it:

php artisan migrate

Step 2: Allow Mass Assignment

app/Models/Task.php

class Task extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = ['title', 'description', 'is_completed'];
}

Step 3: Create the Resource Controller

php artisan make:controller TaskController --resource

Step 4: Register the Route

routes/web.php

use App\Http\Controllers\TaskController;

Route::resource('tasks', TaskController::class);

Step 5: Build the Controller Logic

app/Http/Controllers/TaskController.php

use App\Models\Task;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;

class TaskController extends Controller
{
    public function index()
    {
        $tasks = Task::latest()->get();
        return view('tasks.index', compact('tasks'));
    }

    public function create()
    {
        return view('tasks.create');
    }

    public function store(Request $request)
    {
        $request->validate([
            'title' => 'required|max:255',
        ]);

        Task::create($request->all());

        return redirect()->route('tasks.index')->with('success', 'Task created!');
    }

    public function edit(Task $task)
    {
        return view('tasks.edit', compact('task'));
    }

    public function update(Request $request, Task $task)
    {
        $request->validate(['title' => 'required|max:255']);
        $task->update($request->all());

        return redirect()->route('tasks.index')->with('success', 'Task updated!');
    }

    public function destroy(Task $task)
    {
        $task->delete();
        return redirect()->route('tasks.index')->with('success', 'Task deleted!');
    }
}

Note: edit(Task $task) uses route model binding — Laravel automatically fetches the matching Task from the database based on the route's ID parameter.

Step 6: Build the Views

resources/views/tasks/index.blade.php

@extends('layouts.app')

@section('content')
    <h1>My Tasks</h1>

    @if (session('success'))
        <p>{{ session('success') }}</p>
    @endif

    <a href="{{ route('tasks.create') }}">+ New Task</a>

    <ul>
        @forelse ($tasks as $task)
            <li>
                {{ $task->title }}
                <a href="{{ route('tasks.edit', $task) }}">Edit</a>
                <form action="{{ route('tasks.destroy', $task) }}" method="POST" style="display:inline">
                    @csrf
                    @method('DELETE')
                    <button type="submit">Delete</button>
                </form>
            </li>
        @empty
            <p>No tasks yet.</p>
        @endforelse
    </ul>
@endsection

resources/views/tasks/create.blade.php

@extends('layouts.app')

@section('content')
    <h1>New Task</h1>

    <form action="{{ route('tasks.store') }}" method="POST">
        @csrf
        <input type="text" name="title" placeholder="Task title">
        <textarea name="description" placeholder="Description"></textarea>
        <button type="submit">Save Task</button>
    </form>
@endsection

resources/views/tasks/edit.blade.php

@extends('layouts.app')

@section('content')
    <h1>Edit Task</h1>

    <form action="{{ route('tasks.update', $task) }}" method="POST">
        @csrf
        @method('PUT')
        <input type="text" name="title" value="{{ $task->title }}">
        <textarea name="description">{{ $task->description }}</textarea>
        <button type="submit">Update Task</button>
    </form>
@endsection

Step 7: Test It

php artisan serve

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks — you now have a fully working CRUD app: you can create, view, edit, and delete tasks.

Key Concepts Recap

Concept Where It's Used Route model binding edit(Task $task) @csrf Every form (security) @method('PUT') / @method('DELETE') Forms only support GET/POST natively Validation $request->validate() Redirect with flash message ->with('success', ...)

What's Next?

Your app currently lets anyone create or delete tasks. Next, we'll add a login and registration system so only authenticated users can manage their own data.

title: Laravel Eloquent ORM Tutorial for Beginners
excerpt: Master Laravel Eloquent ORM with this comprehensive beginner's guide. Learn how to simplify database interactions using expressive PHP models, perform CRUD operations, manage complex relationships, and optimize performance with eager loading.
content:
Eloquent is Laravel's built-in ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). It lets you interact with your database using expressive PHP code instead of writing raw SQL queries. This tutorial covers everything a beginner needs to start querying and managing data with Eloquent.

What is an ORM?

An ORM maps your database tables to PHP classes. Each table gets a corresponding "Model," and each row in that table becomes an instance of that model. Instead of writing:

SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > 100;

You write:

Product::where('price', '>', 100)->get();

Creating a Model

php artisan make:model Product

You can generate the model and its migration together:

php artisan make:model Product -m

This creates app/Models/Product.php.

A Basic Eloquent Model

namespace App\Models;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;

class Product extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = ['name', 'description', 'price'];
}

The $fillable array whitelists which fields can be mass-assigned (important for security).

Retrieving Records

// Get all products
$products = Product::all();

// Get one product by ID
$product = Product::find(1);

// Get the first matching record
$product = Product::where('price', '>', 100)->first();

// Get multiple matching records
$products = Product::where('price', '>', 100)->get();

Creating Records

$product = new Product();
$product->name = 'Wireless Mouse';
$product->price = 25.99;
$product->save();

Or using mass assignment:

Product::create([
    'name' => 'Wireless Mouse',
    'price' => 25.99,
]);

Updating Records

$product = Product::find(1);
$product->price = 19.99;
$product->save();

Deleting Records

$product = Product::find(1);
$product->delete();

Query Builder Methods You'll Use Often

Method Purpose ->where() Filter results ->orderBy() Sort results ->take(5) Limit results ->count() Count matching rows ->paginate(10) Paginate results ->first() Get the first match

Defining Relationships

Eloquent makes it easy to connect related tables.

One-to-Many (hasMany / belongsTo)

A User has many Posts:

// In User.php
public function posts()
{
    return $this->hasMany(Post::class);
}

// In Post.php
public function user()
{
    return $this->belongsTo(User::class);
}

Usage:

$user = User::find(1);
$posts = $user->posts; // all posts by this user

$post = Post::find(1);
$author = $post->user; // the user who wrote it

Many-to-Many

// In Product.php
public function categories()
{
    return $this->belongsToMany(Category::class);
}

This requires a pivot table (e.g., category_product) linking the two.

Eager Loading (Avoiding Performance Issues)

// Inefficient (N+1 query problem)
$posts = Post::all();
foreach ($posts as $post) {
    echo $post->user->name;
}

// Efficient
$posts = Post::with('user')->get();

with() loads related data in a single extra query instead of one query per row — a critical performance habit to build early.

What's Next?

You now know how to define, query, and relate your data. It's time to put it all together and build your first real feature: a full CRUD application.

title: Laravel Migrations Tutorial: Managing Your Database Schema
excerpt: Master Laravel Migrations to manage your database schema using version-controlled PHP code. Learn how to create tables, modify existing structures, handle foreign key relationships, and streamline team deployments with essential Artisan commands.
content:
Migrations let you define your database structure using PHP code instead of manually creating tables in phpMyAdmin or a database GUI. This means your entire team (and every environment — local, staging, production) can share the exact same database structure through version control.

Why Use Migrations?

  • Your database schema is tracked in Git, alongside your code

  • Easy to undo changes with rollback

  • Teammates can rebuild the exact same database structure with one command

  • No more manually re-creating tables when setting up a new environment

Setting Up Your Database Connection

Before running migrations, configure your .env file:

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=3306
DB_DATABASE=laravel_app
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=

Creating a Migration

php artisan make:migration create_products_table

This generates a timestamped file in database/migrations/.

Anatomy of a Migration File

use Illuminate\Database\Migrations\Migration;
use Illuminate\Database\Schema\Blueprint;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schema;

return new class extends Migration
{
    public function up(): void
    {
        Schema::create('products', function (Blueprint $table) {
            $table->id();
            $table->string('name');
            $table->text('description')->nullable();
            $table->decimal('price', 8, 2);
            $table->timestamps();
        });
    }

    public function down(): void
    {
        Schema::dropIfExists('products');
    }
};

  • up() – defines what happens when the migration runs

  • down() – defines how to reverse it (used when rolling back)

Common Column Types

Method Column Type $table->id() Auto-incrementing primary key $table->string('name') VARCHAR $table->text('description') TEXT $table->integer('quantity') INTEGER $table->decimal('price', 8, 2) DECIMAL $table->boolean('is_active') BOOLEAN $table->date('published_at') DATE $table->timestamps() Adds created_at and updated_at

Running Migrations

php artisan migrate

This creates all pending tables in your database.

Rolling Back Migrations

php artisan migrate:rollback

Undoes the most recent batch of migrations.

Resetting and Re-running Everything

php artisan migrate:fresh

Drops all tables and re-runs every migration from scratch — useful during development, never run this in production.

Adding a Column to an Existing Table

php artisan make:migration add_stock_to_products_table --table=products

public function up(): void
{
    Schema::table('products', function (Blueprint $table) {
        $table->integer('stock')->default(0);
    });
}

public function down(): void
{
    Schema::table('products', function (Blueprint $table) {
        $table->dropColumn('stock');
    });
}

Foreign Keys (Relationships Between Tables)

Schema::create('orders', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->foreignId('product_id')->constrained()->onDelete('cascade');
    $table->timestamps();
});

This links the orders table to products and automatically deletes related orders if a product is deleted.

Checking Migration Status

php artisan migrate:status

What's Next?

Now that your tables exist, you need a clean way to interact with them in PHP. That's exactly what Laravel's Eloquent ORM does.

title: Laravel Controllers Explained: Creating and Using Them
excerpt: Master Laravel controllers to organize your application logic. This practical guide covers creating controllers with Artisan, routing, dependency injection, and building clean CRUD operations with Resource Controllers.
content:
Controllers keep your application logic organized by moving it out of your routes file and into dedicated classes. This tutorial explains what controllers are, how to create them, and the common patterns you'll use daily.

Why Use Controllers?

Defining logic directly in routes/web.php works fine for small examples, but it quickly becomes unmanageable. Controllers group related logic (e.g., everything related to "products") into a single, organized class.

Creating a Controller

Use Artisan to generate one:

php artisan make:controller ProductController

This creates app/Http/Controllers/ProductController.php.

A Basic Controller Method

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

class ProductController extends Controller
{
    public function index()
    {
        return view('products.index');
    }
}

Connecting a Controller to a Route

use App\Http\Controllers\ProductController;

Route::get('/products', [ProductController::class, 'index']);

Now visiting /products runs the index method and returns the view.

Passing Data to the View

public function index()
{
    $products = [
        ['name' => 'Laptop', 'price' => 1200],
        ['name' => 'Mouse', 'price' => 25],
    ];

    return view('products.index', ['products' => $products]);
}

Resource Controllers (CRUD in One Command)

Laravel can generate a controller pre-built with all the standard CRUD methods:

php artisan make:controller ProductController --resource

This creates seven methods automatically:

Method Purpose HTTP Verb index() List all records GET create() Show "create new" form GET store() Save a new record POST show() Show one record GET edit() Show "edit" form GET update() Update a record PUT/PATCH destroy() Delete a record DELETE

Registering a Resource Route

Instead of writing seven separate routes, register them all in one line:

Route::resource('products', ProductController::class);

Run php artisan route:list to see all seven routes it just generated.

Single Action Controllers

If a controller only handles one task, you can use __invoke() instead of naming a method:

class ShowDashboardController extends Controller
{
    public function __invoke()
    {
        return view('dashboard');
    }
}

Route::get('/dashboard', ShowDashboardController::class);

Injecting the Request Object

Controllers commonly need access to incoming form or query data:

use Illuminate\Http\Request;

public function store(Request $request)
{
    $name = $request->input('name');
    // save it...
}

Best Practices

  • Keep controller methods short — move heavy logic into models or dedicated service classes

  • Use resource controllers whenever you're building standard CRUD features

  • Name methods consistently (index, store, update, etc.) so your code stays predictable

What's Next?

Controllers need data to work with — and that data lives in your database. Next, we'll learn how to define your database tables using Laravel migrations.

title: Laravel Blade Templates: A Beginner's Guide
excerpt: Master Laravel's powerful templating engine with this beginner's guide. Learn how to streamline your views using Blade syntax, including data rendering, conditional logic, loops, layout inheritance, and reusable components.
content:
Blade is Laravel's built-in templating engine. It lets you write clean, readable HTML mixed with dynamic PHP logic — without the ugly <?php ?> tags scattered everywhere. This guide covers everything you need to start building pages with Blade.

Where Blade Files Live

Blade templates are stored in resources/views/ and use the .blade.php extension, e.g., resources/views/home.blade.php.

Displaying Data

Use double curly braces to output a variable safely (Blade automatically escapes it to prevent XSS attacks):

<h1>Welcome, {{ $name }}</h1>

Passing Data From a Route or Controller

Route::get('/welcome', function () {
    return view('welcome', ['name' => 'Kareem']);
});

<h1>Hello, {{ $name }}</h1>

Conditionals

@if ($user->isAdmin)
    <p>Welcome, Admin!</p>
@elseif ($user->isEditor)
    <p>Welcome, Editor!</p>
@else
    <p>Welcome, Guest!</p>
@endif

Loops

@foreach ($products as $product)
    <li>{{ $product->name }}</li>
@endforeach

Blade also supports @for, @while, and @forelse (useful for showing a fallback message when a list is empty):

@forelse ($products as $product)
    <li>{{ $product->name }}</li>
@empty
    <p>No products found.</p>
@endforelse

Layouts: Avoiding Repeated HTML

Instead of repeating your <html>, <head>, and navigation on every page, create a master layout.

resources/views/layouts/app.blade.php

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>@yield('title')</title>
</head>
<body>
    @include('partials.nav')

    <main>
        @yield('content')
    </main>
</body>
</html>

resources/views/home.blade.php

@extends('layouts.app')

@section('title', 'Home Page')

@section('content')
    <h1>Welcome to my site</h1>
@endsection

Including Partial Views

Break repeated UI pieces (like a navbar or footer) into their own files:

@include('partials.footer')

Blade Components (Reusable UI Pieces)

Components are ideal for things like buttons or cards you'll reuse across your app.

Create one with Artisan:

php artisan make:component Alert

Use it anywhere:

<x-alert type="success" message="Saved successfully!" />

Comments in Blade

{{-- This comment will not appear in the rendered HTML --}}

Common Blade Directives Cheat Sheet

Directive Purpose {{ $var }} Output escaped data {!! $var !!} Output raw, unescaped HTML @if / @endif Conditional logic @foreach / @endforeach Loop through data @extends Inherit a layout @section / @yield Define/insert content blocks @include Insert a partial view @csrf Add CSRF token to forms

What's Next?

Now that you can build and display pages, let's move the logic for handling requests out of web.php and into proper Controllers — the "C" in MVC.

title: Laravel Routing Tutorial: GET, POST, and Route Parameters
excerpt: Master the fundamentals of Laravel routing in this comprehensive guide. Learn how to define GET and POST routes, implement dynamic route parameters, utilize named routes, and organize your application structure with route groups and controllers.
content:
Routing is how Laravel decides what code to run when someone visits a specific URL. This tutorial covers everything a beginner needs to define and manage routes confidently.

Where Routes Live

Web routes are defined in routes/web.php. Every route maps a URL to a response — either directly, or via a controller.

Your First Route

Route::get('/', function () {
    return 'Hello, Laravel!';
});

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/ and you'll see "Hello, Laravel!" on screen.

Returning a View Instead of Text

Route::get('/about', function () {
    return view('about');
});

This looks for a file at resources/views/about.blade.php and renders it.

GET vs POST Routes

  • GET – used for retrieving/displaying data (visiting a page)

  • POST – used for submitting data (like a form)

Route::get('/contact', function () {
    return view('contact');
});

Route::post('/contact', function () {
    // handle form submission
});

Every POST request in Laravel requires CSRF protection — Blade handles this automatically with @csrf inside your <form> tag.

Route Parameters

You can capture parts of the URL as variables:

Route::get('/user/{id}', function ($id) {
    return 'User ID: ' . $id;
});

Visiting /user/5 will output "User ID: 5".

Optional Parameters

Route::get('/user/{name?}', function ($name = 'Guest') {
    return 'Hello, ' . $name;
});

Named Routes

Naming routes lets you reference them elsewhere in your app without hardcoding URLs:

Route::get('/dashboard', function () {
    return view('dashboard');
})->name('dashboard');

In a Blade file, you can then link to it like this:

<a href="{{ route('dashboard') }}">Dashboard</a>

If the URL ever changes, you only update it in one place.

Routing to Controllers

As your app grows, you'll move logic out of web.php and into controllers:

use App\Http\Controllers\ProductController;

Route::get('/products', [ProductController::class, 'index']);

Route Groups

Group related routes together to share attributes like a URL prefix or middleware:

Route::prefix('admin')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/dashboard', function () {
        return 'Admin Dashboard';
    });
    Route::get('/settings', function () {
        return 'Admin Settings';
    });
});

This creates /admin/dashboard and /admin/settings.

Applying Middleware to Routes

Route::get('/profile', function () {
    return 'Your Profile';
})->middleware('auth');

This ensures only logged-in users can access /profile. We'll cover middleware in detail in a later article.

Viewing All Registered Routes

Laravel gives you a handy Artisan command to list every route in your app:

php artisan route:list

Summary

Concept Purpose Route::get() Display pages Route::post() Handle form submissions {parameter} Capture dynamic URL segments ->name() Reference routes by name Route::prefix()->group() Organize related routes ->middleware() Restrict access to routes

What's Next?

Now that you understand how to route requests, let's learn how to actually display dynamic content to users using Laravel's templating engine: Blade.

title: Laravel Folder Structure Explained for Beginners
excerpt: New to Laravel? Navigate the framework with confidence. This guide breaks down the essential Laravel folder structure, explaining the core roles of the app, routes, database, and resources directories to help you streamline your development workflow.
content:
When you open a fresh Laravel project, the number of folders can feel overwhelming. This guide breaks down exactly what you need to know as a beginner — and which folders you'll actually touch on a daily basis.

The Root Directory Overview

example-app/
├── app/
├── bootstrap/
├── config/
├── database/
├── public/
├── resources/
├── routes/
├── storage/
├── tests/
├── vendor/
├── .env
└── artisan

Let's go through the important ones.

app/ — Your Application's Core Logic

This is where you'll spend most of your time. Key subfolders:

  • app/Models/ – your Eloquent models (represent database tables)

  • app/Http/Controllers/ – handle incoming requests and return responses

  • app/Http/Middleware/ – code that runs before/after requests (e.g., authentication checks)

  • app/Providers/ – service providers that configure your app on boot

routes/ — Where URLs Are Defined

  • routes/web.php – routes for your website's pages (returns HTML)

  • routes/api.php – routes for your API (returns JSON)

  • routes/console.php – custom Artisan commands

As a beginner, you'll mainly work in web.php at first.

resources/ — Views, CSS, and JavaScript

  • resources/views/ – your Blade template files (the HTML your users see)

  • resources/css/ and resources/js/ – your frontend assets, compiled via Vite

database/ — Migrations, Seeders, and Factories

  • database/migrations/ – version-controlled files that define your database tables

  • database/seeders/ – files used to populate your database with sample/test data

  • database/factories/ – used to generate fake data for testing

config/ — Application Configuration

Contains files like database.php, app.php, and mail.php that control how Laravel behaves. Most values here pull from your .env file rather than being hardcoded.

public/ — The Entry Point

This is the only folder that's publicly accessible from a browser. It contains index.php, the single file that all requests are routed through, plus compiled CSS/JS and images.

storage/ — Logs, Cache, and Uploaded Files

  • storage/logs/ – application error logs (great for debugging)

  • storage/app/ – user-uploaded files

  • storage/framework/ – cached views, sessions, etc.

.env — Environment Configuration

This file holds sensitive and environment-specific settings: database credentials, mail settings, API keys, and your app's debug mode. It's never committed to version control (Git) for security reasons.

artisan — The Command-Line Tool

Not a folder, but worth mentioning: artisan is the file that powers Laravel's command-line interface. You'll use commands like:

php artisan make:controller
php artisan migrate
php artisan serve

Folders You Can Ignore as a Beginner

  • vendor/ – third-party packages managed by Composer (never edit manually)

  • bootstrap/ – low-level framework bootstrapping (rarely touched)

  • tests/ – automated test files (important later, not day one)

Summary Table

Folder What It's For How Often You'll Use It app/ Controllers, models, logic Daily routes/ URL definitions Daily resources/views/ HTML/Blade templates Daily database/migrations/ Database structure Frequently config/ App settings Occasionally public/ Public entry point Rarely

What's Next?

Now that you know your way around a Laravel project, it's time to learn how URLs actually connect to your code. Up next: routing.

title: How to Install Laravel: Step-by-Step Setup Guide (2026)
excerpt: Master the latest Laravel installation methods for 2026. This comprehensive guide covers setting up your local environment, configuring Composer, and launching your first project using both the Laravel Installer and CLI, ensuring a seamless start to your backend development journey.
content:
Before you can start building with Laravel, you need to set up your local development environment. This guide walks you through installing Laravel from scratch, even if you've never used Composer before.

Prerequisites

Before installing Laravel, make sure you have:

  • PHP 8.2 or higher installed

  • Composer – PHP's dependency manager

  • A local server environment (optional, since Laravel has its own built-in server)

  • A code editor (VS Code is recommended)

Checking if PHP and Composer Are Installed

Open your terminal and run:

php -v
composer -v

If both commands return version numbers, you're ready to go. If not, install PHP from php.net and Composer from getcomposer.org.

Option 1: Install Laravel via Composer (Recommended)

Run the following command in your terminal:

composer create-project laravel/laravel example-app

This downloads Laravel and all its dependencies into a folder called example-app.

Option 2: Install Using the Laravel Installer

You can also install the global Laravel installer once, then reuse it for every new project:

composer global require laravel/installer
laravel new example-app

During installation, Laravel will ask if you want to include tools like Breeze (authentication), Pest (testing), or a specific database. As a beginner, you can skip these for now and add them later.

Starting the Development Server

Navigate into your project folder and run:

cd example-app
php artisan serve

You should see output like:

INFO  Server running on [http://127.0.0.1:8000].

Open that URL in your browser — you'll see the default Laravel welcome page. That means Laravel is installed and running correctly.

Alternative: Using Laravel Herd or XAMPP

If you prefer a full local server stack:

  • Laravel Herd (Mac/Windows) – a lightweight, one-click Laravel dev environment

  • XAMPP/WAMP – traditional local server stacks; you'll still use Composer to create the project inside the htdocs folder

Common Installation Errors and Fixes

Error Fix composer: command not found Reinstall Composer and add it to your system PATH PHP version too low Update PHP to 8.2+ zip extension missing Enable the zip extension in your php.ini file Blank page on localhost Make sure you're using php artisan serve, not opening the file directly

What's Next?

title: What is Laravel? A Beginner's Guide to the PHP Framework
excerpt: Discover why Laravel is the industry-standard PHP framework. This beginner's guide explores how Laravel's MVC architecture, Eloquent ORM, and Artisan CLI streamline web development, helping you build secure, scalable applications faster than ever.
content:
If you've started learning PHP and keep hearing the word "Laravel," you're in the right place. This article explains exactly what Laravel is, why it exists, and why it's often the first framework recommended to PHP beginners.

What is Laravel?

Laravel is a free, open-source PHP framework created by Taylor Otwell in 2011. A framework is essentially a toolkit of pre-built code that handles common, repetitive tasks — like connecting to a database, handling forms, managing user logins, and rendering web pages — so you don't have to write everything from scratch.

Instead of writing raw PHP for every single feature of your website, Laravel gives you an organized structure and ready-made tools to build web applications faster, cleaner, and more securely.

Why Not Just Use Plain PHP?

You can build a website with plain PHP, but as your project grows, plain PHP code tends to become messy and hard to maintain. Laravel solves this by enforcing good structure through the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern:

  • Model – handles your data and database logic

  • View – handles what the user sees (the HTML)

  • Controller – handles the logic that connects models and views

This separation makes your code easier to read, test, and scale — especially valuable once you're working on a team or a larger app.

Key Features That Make Laravel Popular

  • Eloquent ORM – lets you interact with your database using PHP code instead of raw SQL

  • Blade Templating Engine – a clean, simple way to build dynamic HTML pages

  • Artisan CLI – a command-line tool that automates repetitive tasks (creating files, running migrations, etc.)

  • Built-in Authentication – login, registration, and password reset systems ready out of the box

  • Routing System – a simple, readable way to map URLs to your application logic

  • Huge Ecosystem – tools like Laravel Breeze, Livewire, Forge, and Nova extend Laravel for almost any use case

Who is Laravel For?

Laravel is a great starting point if you:

  • Already know basic PHP syntax (variables, functions, loops, arrays)

  • Want to build real-world apps like blogs, e-commerce sites, dashboards, or APIs

  • Want a framework with excellent documentation and a large, active community

  • Plan to eventually work as a professional PHP/web developer (Laravel is one of the most in-demand PHP skills)

What Can You Build With Laravel?

  • Content management systems

  • E-commerce platforms

  • SaaS applications

  • REST APIs for mobile apps

  • Admin dashboards

  • Booking and reservation systems

Laravel vs Other PHP Frameworks

Framework Best For Learning Curve Laravel General-purpose web apps, APIs, beginners Beginner-friendly Symfony Enterprise-level, highly customizable apps Steeper CodeIgniter Lightweight, simple projects Beginner-friendly but fewer features

Laravel strikes a strong balance between power and simplicity, which is exactly why it's the most popular PHP framework today.

Final Thoughts

Laravel takes care of the repetitive, tedious parts of web development so you can focus on building features. In the next article in this series, we'll get Laravel installed on your machine and create your very first project.
